Encoding a 200-turn history (BenchmarkAnthropicRequest200Turns, BenchmarkCompletionsRequest200Turns): with the message cache 51 -> 7 and 46 -> 6 allocations per request, without it 2641 -> 2605 and 635 -> 606; mean time per request over ten runs 0.28 ms against 0.31 ms (completions, message cache), 0.33 ms against 0.33 ms (Anthropic, message cache), 0.92 ms against 0.90 ms (completions) and 1.50 ms against 1.49 ms (Anthropic) without it.
- Anthropic message threads are now on by default for any provider whose base URL is on `api.anthropic.com`, not only the `anthropic` provider, as in Pi. Other endpoints still need `compat.supportsMessageThreads`. <!-- fix: 0f8866ca3e65eadeda37f53f0d421646e31a9af8 -->
- Anthropic message threads are now on by default for any provider whose base URL is on `api.anthropic.com`, not only the `anthropic` provider, as in Pi. Other endpoints still need `compat.supportsMessageThreads`. <!-- fix: 704bed4d93 -->
- `ai.GetCacheWarmingRequestOptions` takes the request's context first, `(signal, options)`, like every Go call that is cancellable; it was `(options, signal)`.
- `tui.NewOAuthSelectorComponentAnimated` takes Pi's constructor order, `(mode, providers, onSelect, onCancel, initialSearch, ui)`, with the `tui.TUI` whose `RequestRender` the brand animation calls where it took a bare render function first.
- `coding.BuildModel("provider/id", services)` returns the error `Model not found: provider/id` for an id nothing lists, as Pi does, instead of a model for it; it returns the model the registry lists for an id it does list. A program that wants a custom id on a provider uses `coding.BuildFallbackModel`, the copy of one of the provider's models that `--model` makes.
- The named set-model of the Go, Python, Rust and Lisp extension SDKs (`SetModelNamed`, a `provider/id` string) is a lookup of a listed model: an id nothing lists is the error `Model not found: provider/id` and the session keeps its model. To set a custom model, pass a full model object, as with Pi's `pi.setModel(model)`.
- The `pig` binary is a further 16,384 bytes smaller on Linux amd64, 16,512 on macOS arm64 and 15,872 on Windows amd64 (stripped): the screen writer asks the width package the binary already holds whether a Latin, Greek or Cyrillic letter is of ambiguous East Asian width, so a second width table (`golang.org/x/text/width`) is no longer linked. The answers are the same for every letter it can ask about.
- The `pig` binary is 65,536 bytes smaller on Linux amd64 and 68,608 bytes smaller on Windows amd64 (61,890,720 to 61,825,184 and 63,603,712 to 63,535,104 bytes, stripped): three sorts that run once per command no longer compile their own copy of the sort. They are the drift list of `pig extension upgrade` (24,576 and 29,696 bytes), the target list of `pig piglet publish` with the keys of the project trust store (12,288 and 11,264 bytes), and the field table of the extension SDK's JSON encoder (28,672 and 27,648 bytes). Each writes the same order as before.
- The `pig` binary is a further 278,528 bytes smaller on Linux amd64 and 289,792 bytes smaller on Windows amd64 (to 61,546,656 and 63,245,312 bytes, stripped): it no longer links the package initializers of Go's type checker (`go/types`), which its import of the extension SDK's `upgrade` package had kept. `pig extension upgrade` is unchanged: the type check already ran in the SDK's driver program. The Go extension SDK gains the package `extensions/sdk/upgrade/plan`, the plan, the rules and the drift classification without the type check; `extensions/sdk/upgrade` keeps every name.
- The release binary is 24,576 B smaller on linux/amd64 and 25,088 B smaller on windows/amd64: the plugin UI registry sorts its mounts and the members of a canonical JSON object with the shared sort of `internal/sortx`, so two copies of the sort that came with the registry are no longer linked.
- models: an availability pass (the refresh behind the model list, and the provider count and model list the interactive mode reads at start and after a login) checks the revision of auth.json once instead of 4 to 5 times per provider: an interactive start makes 19 revision stats where it made 455. A write to auth.json during a pass is used by the next request and the next pass; a write through the credential API in the same process is used at once, and a `!command` key is still evaluated on every read. An extension provider whose own auth check rewrites auth.json on disk is seen by the next request and the next pass rather than by the rest of the same pass (D628).
- A model request that cache warming skips (warming off, a request that cannot be replayed, a model without a cache lifetime) no longer copies the session's message list: 64 bytes per message once per request, 0.8 % of the bytes a 20-prompt session allocates.
- A message kept from an OpenAI-compatible completions stream no longer holds the line buffers its response id, finish reason and tool call ids and names were read from: the message keeps its own copy of those four short strings. In the audit's 20-prompt session that was 280 buffers, 61 KB of the memory in use at rest.
- A prompt no longer copies the parameter schema of every declared tool three times. The compaction estimate reads the session's current system message in place instead of replaying a deep copy of it, a compaction is prepared from the entries' own messages and copies only the ones it hands to extension handlers and the summarizer, and the loadout comparison before each request reads a built-in tool's schema in place instead of rebuilding it. In a session with the four default tools and three extension tools of 12 properties each, a prompt allocates about 121 KB and 815 objects less (490 KB and 3,240 allocations before, 370 KB and 2,420 after). The request bodies sent to each provider, what an extension handler may edit, and the re-declaration of a tool an extension re-registers are unchanged.
- A streamed response is searched for reasoning markers only when a keepalive asks. The idle-timeout tracker for server-sent events (D131) counts a comment line or a ping as progress while the last event was a reasoning event; it searched every data line for the providers' reasoning markers and now searches only the line a keepalive follows. The timeout ends the same streams at the same time. On the fake-model benchmark (paired runs against the base, 8 rounds) user instructions per prompt fell by 1.1 % for a headless prompt (8 of 8 pairs), 1.6 % in a 40-prompt interactive session (7 of 8) and 0.7 % in a 20-prompt session (5 of 8, inside that cell's noise); CPU and wall time stayed inside the noise.
- Loading a session decodes its messages faster, with the same result: a message was checked for well-formed JSON once for its record and again for its content and for each content block it holds, and now once. A 20 KB tool result and a 6 KB answer decode in 464 µs instead of 678 µs (-32%); a resumed session of 4,000 entries starts that much sooner.
- A streamed response costs less CPU in a short session. Every read of the response body that waited for the network asked for the calling goroutine's ID, which formats the goroutine's stack header (25 microseconds) until 17 distinct goroutines have asked, so the first requests of a session paid it on each chunk: 15% of the CPU profile of a 400 KB write call's response. The read now compares the goroutine's runtime record address (1.8 nanoseconds, no proof needed) with the one it recorded.
- A long answer that streams in allocates about half as much per frame. Each frame copied the answer's whole row list twice into new arrays (the Markdown block's rows, then the message's), 88 MB of the 255 MB a 60,000-character answer allocates, which made the collector run 48 times where 0.7.0 ran 41. A container that holds a Markdown block or an assistant message now borrows its rows from an array the child keeps for its next render, as it already borrows a nested container's. What a frame draws is unchanged. BenchmarkInteractiveLongAnswerStream (benchstat, count 12 interleaved, one core): 89.3 to 48.2 KB a chunk (-46%), 356 to 293 ms an answer (-17.7%, p=0.000). In the harness's 60,000-character answer: 27 collections and 1.67 s of user CPU (0.7.0: 41 and 1.88 s; before: 48 and 2.20 s; medians of 8 interleaved rounds).
- A streamed delta in a long session costs less. Each frame used to ask every message and tool card of the transcript whether it had changed, which at 4,000 entries took about 75 microseconds of a 190-microsecond frame. A container now reads the invalidations of its children of the transcript's own types (spacers, text, user and assistant messages, and tool cards whose tool has finished) and asks only the others, so the frame at 4,000 entries costs 114 instead of 188 microseconds (a 1,000-entry transcript: 98 instead of 118; an empty one is unchanged). What the frame draws is unchanged.
- A write call that streams a long file in no longer stalls the frame that completes it. The card draws the highlighted lines of the whole file once the call is complete; for a 400 KB TypeScript file that single highlight stopped the screen for about 300 ms. While the content streams in, the card now highlights the whole file a step at a time (a step is 32 KB), so the last frame highlights only what the last step left. The lines the card draws are the same ones a single run over the whole file gives. A step makes one frame longer, so the steps are few enough (a 400 KB file has twelve, under 1% of its frames) that the 99th-percentile frame gap stays at the 18-20 ms it was. In the Pi-Bolt `pauses.py` harness (pinned core, interleaved rounds) the longest stall of the 50 KB, 200 KB and 400 KB files went from 93, 252-271 and 310-366 ms to 59-69, 84-97 and 90-93 ms.
- A large tool-result text (4 KiB or more) is escaped to JSON once: the `read` tool's structured result, the session entry that records the text and the request that sends it share one cached encoding, where each escaped the text on its own. A long session with four file reads per prompt runs about 12 % fewer user-mode instructions per prompt and about 5 % less CPU time (paired `perf stat`, 10 sessions each; CPU time per prompt 38.8 ms to 36.3 ms at 20 prompts, 46.2 ms to 44.3 ms at 40), and a one-prompt headless run about 13 % fewer. The bytes of the tool event, the session file and the request body are unchanged. The encodings a read makes before a request uses them are held to 4 MiB, so a process that reads files and sends no request keeps a few MiB, not the request cache's 64 MiB limit.
- An interactive run collects garbage at a GC percent of 150 until more than 8 MiB of heap is live, then at the default 100 (D621), unless `GOGC` or `GOMEMLIMIT` is set. It cuts the CPU of the interactive and default-theme start-up scenarios by 6-8 % and of a long session by about 3 % per prompt, for about 1.6 MB more peak memory in a short session; a session past 8 MiB live is unchanged. <!-- change: 92630fc35 -->
- The agent's question "does any extension handle this event?", asked for every streamed message update and every provider stream event, no longer takes the extension lock, builds a handler list and allocates: the extension keeps a lock-free set of the events it has handlers for, republished when a handler is added, removed or replaced. A 40-prompt interactive session executes about 1.8 % fewer instructions per prompt (6 paired sessions, 6 of 6 with fewer); no event, order or request changes.
- A write call that streams in, and a TypeScript or JavaScript code block that streams into an answer, are highlighted from where the last update left off instead of from their first line on every update. Writing a 50 KB TypeScript file takes the terminal 2.9 s of CPU instead of 4.9 s, and the write card's own share falls from 2.6 s to 0.4 s: after every update the first 50 lines were highlighted again as one block, and the last line once more to count the lines. The highlighted lines are the ones a whole run returns, and the card is drawn as before.
- Loading a long session is faster, with the same decoded entries: the JSON reader checks validity in one table-driven pass and finds the end of a nested value without stepping a state machine over every byte, and session lines written with spaces between tokens (by a tool that is not Pi or PiG) no longer take the full canonical rewrite when the spacing is all that differs. Decoding the 4,000 entries of Pi-Bolt's `long_transcript` session takes about 0.17 s of CPU instead of 0.62 s, and the benchmark of one record decode (`BenchmarkDecodeSessionEntryHarnessShape`) takes 37% of the time for compact lines and 29% for spaced ones.
- A long interactive session uses less CPU per prompt: each request finds the large tool results it re-sends by their address even when the conversation holds several equal copies (the same file read again), instead of hashing and comparing them on every turn. In the Pi-Bolt long-session benchmark, CPU per prompt at 40 prompts falls from about 81 to 72 ms on one pinned core. Over a plain `http://` connection (a local model server) the request body also goes out in vectored writes instead of 32 KiB copies, which brings it to about 63 ms; `https://` connections send it as before. The requests sent are the same.
- Rendering a long transcript is faster, with the same output: word wrapping cuts a line into words without copying them (`WrapTextWithAnsi` on a long paragraph takes 26 µs instead of 102 µs and makes 26 allocations instead of 905), and the Markdown inline text rule classifies characters by table. The first fullscreen frame over a resumed session of 1,000 entries costs about 32% less CPU (333 ms to 227 ms); Pi-Bolt's `long_transcript` row (answer streaming into a 4,000-entry session, fullscreen) drops from 0.90 s to 0.48 s of median CPU.
- A spinner step no longer draws a frame of its own while a reply or a tool call is streaming in: the step asks for its frame within 40 ms (or half its interval, if shorter), and a frame the stream asks for in that time draws it. Pi draws one frame per step, which is about one frame in five of a streaming write call. In a tmux pane, where each frame costs the tmux server a read, a parse and a redraw, this saves the server about a fifth of its frames on the `write:50` cell of the Pi-Bolt `tmux_load.py` harness. The settled screen and every other frame are unchanged; a step that no frame draws within the time is still drawn by a frame of its own, and a loader that is not on a PiG renderer asks at once as before. Recorded as D619.
- A finished `read` call no longer encodes the file text up to four times in the interactive screen. The card compares the tool's structured content with the text without making a copy (a stack buffer, a 2 KB step at a time), and the built-in read renderer, which never reads the structured content, is handed the card's result as it is held instead of one rebuilt from the file for each draw. A renderer an extension registers still receives the structured content. The text is scanned eight bytes at a time. On a 150 KB file the comparison allocates nothing where the rebuild allocated the file's size.
- Messages that named Pi as the product that prints them name pig or PiG (divergence record D2, "Product name in messages"): `Session file is not a valid pig session: <path>`, the "another pig session" hints of the ChatGPT sign-in and of a git package update, the tmux `extended-keys-format` warning, the description of the "Show hardware cursor" setting, and the models.json reference page. The extensions link of the extension deprecation warning points at PiG's documentation. The JSON schemas keep Pi's text.
- `pig --help` lists `PIG_OFFLINE`, `PIG_SELF_UPDATE_COMMAND` and `PIG_TELEMETRY`. Pi's `PI_OFFLINE`, `PI_SELF_UPDATE_COMMAND` and `PI_TELEMETRY` keep working.
- Messages of `pig status`, the Piglet commands, the Piglet build and `pig extension init` spell the product PiG where they said Pig, for example `PiG status: healthy`, `PiG runtime: ...` and the `PiG:` line of a signed manifest. A script that matches `Pig status:` must match `PiG status:`.
- The default-model diagnosis says "PiG reads" where it said "Pi reads".
- The address of `examples/ui-view-web/bridge.mjs` works once. It is now `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/#<code>`: the code is in the fragment, which a browser sends in no request and no `Referer`. The page clears it from the address bar at once, posts it in a request body to `/exchange` and keeps the session secret it is answered with in `sessionStorage` (that tab's only; no cookie), sending it as `Authorization: Bearer` on every request, so no address holds a secret after the first load. A code is good for one use and ten minutes; when it is used, or the ten minutes pass, the bridge writes the next one into `open.html` and `address` (mode 0600, in a mode 0700 directory), so open `open.html` again for another tab. A replayed, expired or wrong code is refused, and the page says to open the file again; a tab whose secret the bridge no longer knows says the bridge was restarted. The browser's history may keep the used address, which opens nothing. `--print-token`, or `UI_VIEW_WEB_PRINT_TOKEN=1`, now prints `ui-view-web: http://127.0.0.1:<port>/#<code>`; one run gives one code for one exchange. A script that matched `?token=` matches `/#` instead.
- `examples/ui-view-web/bridge.mjs` no longer prints the page's token. Its first line is now `ui-view-web: http://127.0.0.1:<port>/ (open: <dir>/open.html)`. Open that file (`open <path>` on macOS, `xdg-open <path>` on Linux, `Start-Process <path>` in PowerShell): it sends your browser to the address. The bridge makes the file, and `address` beside it, in a private temporary directory (mode 0700, files 0600) and removes them when it ends. Do not give the content of `address` to a command as an argument: other users of a Linux machine can read process arguments. `--print-token`, or `UI_VIEW_WEB_PRINT_TOKEN=1`, prints the old line, `ui-view-web: http://127.0.0.1:<port>/?token=<token>`. The page now removes the token from the address bar after it loads and keeps it for that tab, the bridge compares the token in constant time and sends `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` and `Cache-Control: no-store`, and it also ends cleanly on SIGHUP.
- `pig` starts with about 500 fewer allocations and 88 KB fewer bytes (Linux, a warm first prompt with a `models.json`): the JSON Schema validator behind `Value.Check` no longer builds its draft tables, format map and message printer when the process starts, the empty cell manifest of a stock `pig` is no longer decoded through reflection, and the provider order of `models.json` is read once for the three startup callers that ask for it.
- A `### Fixed` bullet can state the root cause and the regression tests of its fix after the fix marker, as `<!-- cause: <why the bug happened> -->` and `<!-- tests: <test>[, <test>...] -->`; a fix commit can state them with a `Root-Cause:` trailer and `Regression-Test:` trailers (`.github/CONTRIBUTING.md`). `make bug-ledger-check` now also fails for a fix committed on or after 2026-11-14 for which no root cause can be derived, for an entry whose impact or platform class its text no longer reads as, and for an entry that names a commit `HEAD` does not reach while its fix marker names the commit that replaced it; `make bug-ledger` settles the last two.
- A metadata refresh of the model registry converts the bundled model catalog once where it converted it three times. The composer's model list, its all-models read and the provider model data of a registration each ran every listed model through the catalog conversion; they now share one converted snapshot per provider, built on first read and replaced as a whole when the stripped APIs change, so a reader that began before a refresh keeps the models of the snapshot it loaded and never sees a mix of two. Pi reads the runtime's snapshot in process in the same way. BenchmarkSessionRegistryMetadataRefresh, one processor, 200 iterations, three rounds each, on a loaded 192-processor host (load average 80 to 130): 928 allocations and 138.9 KB per refresh before, 233 allocations and 60.9 KB after; 308 to 353 microseconds before, 72 microseconds after. The start of pig does not get measurably shorter: 30 warm starts in json mode with a Node extension had a median first reply of 311.8 ms before and 316.5 ms after, and 16.5 ms before and 16.6 ms after without an extension, both within the noise of that host.
- A worker thread or a forked child of a Node extension no longer resolves `@earendil-works/pi-ai` (the root and `/compat`, `/models`, `/oauth`, `/providers/all`) when the extension has no copy of the package in its own `node_modules`. It resolved there up to v0.7.0 because PiG started the extension with `--import` of its loader, which a child or worker inherited; since the change that starts the extension without that flag (698d040146, the `process.execArgv` fix) they get none of PiG's module hooks and resolve as they do under Pi, so `import "@earendil-works/pi-ai"` fails there with `Cannot find package '@earendil-works/pi-ai'`. Install the package beside the extension (`npm install @earendil-works/pi-ai`), as under Pi. Where the extension has its own copy, the child and the worker now load that copy, as under Pi, instead of PiG's module; the extension's own process is unchanged. <!-- fix: 698d040146 -->
- Chord's calls in flight survive a hold's `loading` unbind: a hold whose object leaves `live` for `loading` (a restart, a live failure retrying) keeps its calls in flight, and each gets one answer from what it waits on (the instance it runs on, or the object's gate); calls sent by the names the hold was bound with, before the consumer learnt of the `loading`, wait at the gate too. `failed` and removal still reject. <!-- fix: 326b180d8f -->
- Plugins import each other by relative path within a root (copied into the importer's script) and across repositories by package name through the package's `exports`; imports by plugin name (`@app/notes/contract`) are removed, and a relative path leaving the root is a build error.
- Chord: `workers.WorkersBuilt` is the sealed union Pi's `WorkersBuilt` is, `WorkersBuiltBuilt{Inputs}` or `WorkersBuiltFailed{Error}`, each with its `Kind()`, where it was one struct with an `Err` field. `Workers.Build` returns it, `Workers.Built` returns nil for Pi's `undefined` (it returned a pointer), and a caller switches on the variant. The ledger's interface closure now derives `WorkersBuilt`, `StateDefinition` and `StateDefinition.host` as ported (15117 of 15117 interface IDs closed).
- Chord's Go HTTP and workers API takes Pi's shapes where it differed: `Authenticator` and `WorkerPlugins.Load` take the context first, `NodeRequest` is one struct tagged by `Kind` (`NodeRequestRequest` or `NodeRequestRefused`) with a closed `WireStatus`, `SameSite` is the string union `"Strict" | "Lax"`, a contribution's sockets are `HttpSocketEntry{Pattern, Socket HttpSocketOptions}` (`SocketFunc` makes the plain one), `Router.Hosts` and `Router.Framers` are `[]string`, `Workers.State` and `WorkerResult.Busy` are `chord.Watchable[delta.JsonValue]` (`host.Expose` makes one of a reference's member), `Workers.Inputs` is the file list of the worker base, `WorkerLoad.Core` is the app's Go facets (Pi's `core`) and `NodeCore` the JavaScript ones, and `telemetryingest.Batch` is `TelemetryBatch`.
- Chord (Go API): the comment of `store.ByteSource` (`chordsync.SyncBody` is that type) says how long a chunk lasts: it is valid until the next `Next` or `Close`, and a consumer copies it to keep it. The gzip and gunzip bodies of `chord/sync` fill the buffer they handed out again, where Pi's streams hand out arrays of their own, so a consumer that kept its chunks read the bytes of later ones and wrote a batch that did not decode. Tests in `chord/sync` hold both sides: the bodies do reuse the chunk, and nothing in the package that reads a body depends on a chunk past the next `Next`. No behaviour changes.
- Chord: the two vendored chord trees (`chord/nextnode/plugins/node` and `chord/nextnode/surfaces/client`) are made the same way, from the pin plus the carried Pi commits their manifests list (`PI_CARRIED`), and `make vendor-chord-carried-check PI_REPO=<a Pi clone>` proves that each tree is its manifest's commit plus those commits.
- Chord's terminal launcher takes the terminal as `TerminalOptions.Input` and `TerminalOptions.Output`, as Pi's `startTerminal` takes `input` and `output` (raw mode, size and resizes found by method on them) instead of one `Terminal` value; the bridge messages' `Kind` fields are named string types with constants; `tui.OptimisticAdd` returns its call's result as Pi's does (`OptimisticAdd[A, R]`); `tui.TerminalTheme` ports Pi's terminal theme lookup. <!-- change: 9c1e5b7a40 -->
- Chord: `App.Close` no longer waits for the bases' and surfaces' builds or the scan of the server's own code, as Pi's `#close` does (what they finish after the close is dropped; the lock is released at Close return); `App.Wait` joins them for owners that need to (Go lifetime ownership, no Pi counterpart).
- **Breaking (Go API)** `chord/nextnode/app`, `chord/nextnode/surfaces`, `chord/nextnode/workers`, `chord/nextnode/plugins` (Pi `284e63d9`): the server starts off the build path. `StartServer` returns once the server listens; the web and terminal base bundles and each worker kind's base are built right after, from the files as they are then, and the server's own code (its executable) is recorded after them. `App.BasesBuilt()` and `App.BaseWatched()` are channels that close when the bases are built and when the base code is recorded and compared once. `NewWebSurface` and `NewTuiSurface` no longer build: they return a surface with `Build()` and `Built()` (a page, a surface file or a launcher's start waits for the build and answers 503 when it failed; the rollout step waits for it and fails when it did, ending its wait at its context's abort while the build goes on), `WebSurface.Base` and `Inputs` are gone, and `App.Web.Base` and `App.Tui.Base` are now methods, empty until built. `Plugins.WatchBase` returns a channel closing once the record's first comparisons ended. A worker kind's entry that cannot be started no longer fails `CreateWorkers`: `Workers.Build()` copies the entry into a private directory (`WorkersOptions.BaseDir`, the kit's `cache/workers/<kind>/`, emptied first; removed at `Close` once every worker exited) and records its bytes, every worker forks that copy, an edit of the entry marks `base`, and an entry that cannot be started or copied fails the build and every start (`worker failed to start`). The data directory gains `cache/` and `cache/workers/` (`AppLayout.Cache`, `AppLayout.WorkerBases`, mode 0700).
- A base that does not build after the listen is reported as `AppErrorBaseBuild` (`AppError.Base` names `web`, `tui` or the worker kind) and the server runs on. What the app reports after its close is dropped.
- The server's executable changed since the process started (its modification or status-change time after the start, not later than five seconds from now) marks `base` until a restart, as the bytes read may not be the ones running; one stamped in the future is compared by its content alone.
- A worker kind's base is built by one goroutine the component owns, shared by every waiter: a start waits for it only until the component closes, `Close` does not wait for it, and what a build finishes after the close is dropped (the copy is written beside the base directory and committed only while the component is open), so a build that outlives the close never touches a directory the next start owns.
- Chord pages: the language and the theme a user chose earlier are applied when a page opens or reloads. Pi's followers apply a stored pick only at its next change, so the choice looked unsaved after a reload; PiG's apply the value their watch of the pick was acquired with (divergence D636: a patch over Pi's two vendored followers, and the Go ports `FollowActiveLanguage` and `FollowActiveTheme`).
- Chord: a reload restarts every live object of a changed plugin and the calls running at the commit (and every call they cause, over trusted links too) finish on the old code; new calls wait for the new code. A wait that would cycle through its own drain fails at once with `unavailable/reload_cycle`. A call's answer now follows its state over a link. <!-- fix: d892104fad -->
- Chord: `host.get`, `host.hold`, `host.registry` and a root's `ctx.get` made before `host.load` fail `not_ready` at once instead of waiting for a publication nobody started; a plugin name that is no npm name makes `load` and `reload` fail before anything changes. A request that waits unbound after the publication (a type or registry nobody serves, a registry whose first `compose` failed) is reported once through `onError` as `unbound_long` after 5 s, by one host-wide timer; a registry with contributions and no provider is reported as `registry_undeclared` at each publication.
- Chord: `FormatNumber` prints what the pinned Node's `Intl.NumberFormat` prints (symbols, grouping with minimum grouping digits, numbering systems, half-away-from-zero rounding; the review's 312 differing outputs are 0) and `FormatTime` is ported (`TimeOptions`: `timeStyle` short or medium, or hour/minute/second, with `hour12`). Both read tables generated from the pinned Node's ICU (`make intl-tables`, part of `pin-bump`) and return `(string, error)` for what `Intl` throws. A drift test diffs the tables against a live Node.
- Vendored Chord trees (tooling): a change PiG makes to one of Pi's vendored chord files is a patch under `automation/gen/chord-patches` (`<record>-<name>.patch`, a unified diff with Pi's paths). The vendoring scripts apply the patches after the copy and fail when one does not apply exactly (no offset, no fuzz) or when its record is not `SCRUTINIZED:approved`; `chord/nextnode/plugins/node/manifest.json` and `chord/nextnode/surfaces/client/manifest.json` gain `patches` (name and sha256 of each patch applied; an empty list when none), and their file hashes are of the patched files. `make vendor-chord-carried-check` regenerates with the patches.
- Chord's plugins component is split in three packages, so a worker links no esbuild (Pi's `child.test.ts`, "loads no esbuild"; `go list -deps` of the workers package listed 26 esbuild packages before). `chord/nextnode/plugins/model` holds the data and discovery (`Plugin`, `DiscoverPlugins`, `BuiltFacet`, `BuildOptions`, `BaseInputs`, `ContentHash`, `HashFile`), `chord/nextnode/plugins/build` the esbuild builder (`BuildFacet`, `ScopeCSSModule`, `Recorder`), and `chord/nextnode/plugins` the runtime and the component. The component no longer builds by itself: pass `build.BuildFacet` as `PluginsOptions.Build` (and `TestPluginOptions.Build`); `CreatePlugins` panics without it. `build.BuildFacet` does not start the Node subprocess that reads the mapping of a CSS module: pass the evaluator in `BuildOptions.Mappings`, as the component does. Types that moved are named by their new package (`model.Plugin`, `model.PlatformNode`, `model.BaseInputs`, `build.NewRecorder`), with no aliases left in `plugins`.
- Chord sync takes Pi's shapes: `LocalCopy` is a tagged struct (`Kind`), `FlushSchedulerOptions` times are milliseconds (`IntervalMs`, `UrgentMs`, `RetryMs`, `MaxRetryMs`, `SetTimer(callback, delayMs)`, `Now() int64`), `SyncFileSystem.OpenBinaryReader` takes options, `EncodeLogLine` returns the line as a string, and `sync.JsonObject` and `sync.NewLogFormatError` exist.
- Chord: a schema snapshot refuses a map keyed by anything but strings, a func, a chan and an unsafe pointer, naming the path (Go's form of Pi's symbol-key and accessor refusals); `surfaces.InLanguage`, `CurrentLanguage` and `Messages.InScope` carry the render scope in the context (Pi's `inLanguage`, `currentLanguage`, `t`).
- Chord: `HostError` `query_failed` names the query that failed in `Query`, where it named the table in `Table`.
- Raised `github.com/alecthomas/chroma/v2` from 2.24.1 to 2.27.0 (and added its `regexp2/v2` dependency). Only the portlens parity-evidence tool in `automation/` links chroma; `pig` and its syntax highlighting (the highlight.js port) do not, so the shipped binary and highlight output are unchanged.
- Raised `github.com/alecthomas/chroma/v2` from 2.24.1 to 2.27.0 (and added its `regexp2/v2` dependency). Only the portlens parity-evidence tool in `automation/` links chroma; `pig` and its syntax highlighting (the highlight.js port) do not, so the shipped binary and highlight output are unchanged.
- CI: `make module-publication` gives `go mod download` of a nested module 600 seconds instead of 60 (`--download-timeout SECONDS`), because the public module proxy answers a new pseudo-version with a timeout for up to half an hour while it fetches the repository and the direct fallback needs a minute or more under load. A download that still does not finish fails with a message that names the proxy delay and the `.info` URL to poll, instead of a bare timeout.
- CI: a pull request no longer saves the big caches. `ci.yml` and `security.yml` restore the Go build cache, the Go modules, the Cargo registry and test targets, the npm cache and the Durable Cloudflare host's TinyGo and Pi reference with `actions/cache/restore` and save them with `actions/cache/save` only on main (the weekly run, a dispatch) and on a dispatch of a release branch (`CACHE_SAVE`); a pull request or merge queue run falls back to the newest copy that main saved. A pull request's caches are visible to that pull request alone, so one copy of each per pull request filled the repository's cache limit and evicted main's. The Linux jobs that used `setup-go`'s `cache: true` and every `setup-node` `cache: npm` restore the same entries explicitly, so each cache has one copy. Cache diagnosis by @Patrick-Kappen.
- CI: a new `cache-cleanup.yml` deletes the caches of a pull request's merge ref when the pull request closes (token scope `actions: write`, no checkout), and `ci-images.yml` cancels a superseded pull request run while a push to main, the schedule and a publish dispatch still run to the end.
- CI: a pull request no longer saves the big caches. `ci.yml` and `security.yml` restore the Go build cache, the Go modules, the Cargo registry and test targets, the npm cache and the Durable Cloudflare host's TinyGo and Pi reference with `actions/cache/restore` and save them with `actions/cache/save` only on main (the weekly run, a dispatch) and on a dispatch of a release branch (`CACHE_SAVE`); a pull request or merge queue run falls back to the newest copy that main saved. A pull request's caches are visible to that pull request alone, so one copy of each per pull request filled the repository's cache limit and evicted main's. The Linux jobs that used `setup-go`'s `cache: true` and every `setup-node` `cache: npm` restore the same entries explicitly, so each cache has one copy. Cache diagnosis by @Patrick-Kappen.
- CI: a new `cache-cleanup.yml` deletes the caches of a pull request's merge ref when the pull request closes (token scope `actions: write`, no checkout), and `ci-images.yml` cancels a superseded pull request run while a push to main, the schedule and a publish dispatch still run to the end.
- CI: the chord surface tests (`make ci-chord-tui`, `make ci-chord-web`) run in their own job, `Chord surfaces`, instead of as the last two steps of `Node extensions`, as Pi split its chord tests out (Pi #12114). The job sets up Go and current Node only and `CI result` requires it; `test/ci-images/chord_job_test.go` fails when a chord target runs in no job or in two, when the required check does not depend on its job, or when its recipe no longer fails on a missing Node or browser.
- CI: the approval of a divergence or additive record binds a hash of the record's normative text. The `SCRUTINIZED:approved` line carries `text-sha256:<16 hex>` (and a date once the owner approves), and `make divergence-quality`, part of `make check` and of the bookkeeping CI group, fails when the text of an approved record changes without a new approval line, naming the record, the bound hash and the current hash. Evidence blocks (tests, scenarios, call-site markers), inline repository paths and test names, link targets, Pi pin versions, whitespace and wrapping are not in the hash. Only the owner approves a changed text (`make divergence-approve ID=D<N>`); a contributor lists the record in `automation/ci/divergence-reapproval-pending.txt` with a class and a reason, which the gate prints on every run. 61 records are bound to their current text; the 148 whose text changed after their bare, copied marker was first written, or that were added with such a marker, stay listed until the owner approves them again.
- CI: the approval of a divergence or additive record binds a hash of the record's normative text. The `SCRUTINIZED:approved` line carries `text-sha256:<16 hex>` (and a date once the owner approves), and `make divergence-quality`, part of `make check` and of the bookkeeping CI group, fails when the text of an approved record changes without a new approval line, naming the record, the bound hash and the current hash. Evidence blocks (tests, scenarios, call-site markers), inline repository paths and test names, link targets, Pi pin versions, whitespace and wrapping are not in the hash. Only the owner approves a changed text (`make divergence-approve ID=D<N>`); a contributor lists the record in `automation/ci/divergence-reapproval-pending.txt` with a class and a reason, which the gate prints on every run. 80 records are bound to their current text; the 82 whose text changed after their bare, copied marker was first written stay listed until the owner approves them again.
- CI: the pre-flight's `test-expectation` check admits what the line lint admits. A pull request that changes expected values of a Go test together with production code passes when `test/parity/testprune-reviewed.toml` at the PR's head holds a row of that test file whose commit prefix (at least 10 characters) names exactly one commit of the PR, that commit changed the file, and the row passes the lint's validation (CITE to a Pi file main inventories, DIVERGENCE to a record on main or in the PR, NOBEHAVIOR, message-only); the `Pi-Behavior-Change:` trailer in the PR body and a commit still admits it as before. The pre-flight asks the API for the files of each commit a row names (one call per commit, at most 50 commits per PR). Every admission is printed (a log line, a `::notice` annotation and a comment row) and asks for nothing, a ledger or a commit that cannot be fetched or read leaves the check undecided, and a row that does not apply changes nothing. The validation is one package, `automation/ci/preflight/reviewed`, which the line lint calls too. Text of a pull request that the pre-flight prints (a ledger reason or cite, a file name, an error of the API) is now one line in the job log, and a ledger reason or cite in the comment is one code span.
- CI: the pre-flight's `test-expectation` check leaves the `[[tooling]]` directories of `test/testdata-provenance.toml` on main out of its rule, as the line lint does (one shared parser and prefix match). A prefix that only the pull request adds exempts nothing, a list that cannot be read on main fails the check, and each skip is printed.
- CI: the pre-flight prints text of a pull request so that it cannot start a workflow command in either form the runner reads, `::command::` or the legacy `##[command]` (`##[` is printed as `# #[`); an admission notice is stored whole in the record of the verdict and cut only when printed.
- CI: a pre-flight runs first and the full CI waits for it. `.github/workflows/preflight.yml` (Patrick Kappen's engine in `automation/ci/preflight`: commits, DCO and signing, comments, secret scans, lint-class content rules) judges a pull request when it opens or changes and every hour for every open one, records the `preflight` commit status, and `ci.yml`'s new `Pre-flight verdict` job waits for that status before `Bookkeeping` and everything after it; `CI result` fails when the pre-flight rejected the head or never judged it.
- CI: the light pull-request run is one runner. Windows native-1, macOS native and the Node loader move to the queue tier, so a light run (`PIG_PR_CI_LIGHT` `queue` or `label`) runs Linux only. A pull request that changes a path of `automation/ci/os-specific-paths.txt` (`*_windows.go`, `*_darwin.go`, the native platform packages, installers, the Windows and macOS CI definition) runs the full set on every runner, as the `ci:full` label does. The full run also runs nightly on main (it was weekly) and on a push to a `release/**` branch.
- CI: only the nightly run on main (and a dispatch) saves caches. Every `actions/cache` step of `ci.yml` is a restore plus a save under `CACHE_SAVE`, macOS included, `cache-warm.yml` runs only when a lockfile changes, and `cache-prune` keeps the newest PORT_MAP ledger of each shard instead of one for all eight.
- CI: a red nightly starts `nightly-bisect.yml`, which runs CI on the commits between the last green nightly and the red one (a temporary `bisect/*` branch each), names the first bad commit and opens an issue asking for a fix PR; it merges nothing.
- The read tool's streamed read and grep's ripgrep event loop allocate nothing per line or per event: a 140 KB read allocates as often as before it streamed and 41% fewer bytes, and grep's allocations stay constant as its context grows.
- `GrepOperations.readFile` stays a deprecated, optional member that is accepted and never called, in the Go (`GrepOperations.ReadFile`), Python (`read_file`), Rust (`read_file`) and Lisp (`:read-file`) SDKs as in Pi. Grep takes its context lines from ripgrep; to search a remote system, wrap the tool's `execute`. `pig upgrade` no longer deletes the member.
- Compacting a long session now sends fewer summary requests. When the session has provider usage, a history that fits the model's context window together with the summary's output limit is summarized in one request, as in Pi, instead of being split early into several serial requests that each take minutes on a slow model; a longer history is split only as far as a request can hold. The size of a request is the usual estimate scaled by what the provider counted for the session's latest reply, so a request is never sent over the window, and if the provider still refuses one the rest of the history is split as before. A session without provider usage is split as before. <!-- fix: 949305dc9 -->
- While a context summary is being written, the compaction line shows how long it has run and how much of the summary has streamed: `Compacting context... 1m 12s · ~14k tokens (escape to cancel)`. Nothing is shown of the time within the first second, and nothing of the size before the first streamed text. The same applies to auto-compaction and context-overflow compaction. The size is the characters of the summary request in flight divided by four (a retry or the next chunk of a long history starts again from zero). RPC, print and JSON modes are unchanged, and so is every request.
- Reasoning models on `openai-completions` now send system messages (the initial system prompt and mid-conversation system messages) with the `system` role instead of `developer` for Groq, OpenRouter (`openai/*` and `anthropic/*`), Xiaomi, custom `models.json` providers, local servers, and other hosts that omit `compat.supportsDeveloperRole`. Provider `openai` (on any base URL), endpoints whose base URL includes `api.openai.com`, and bare `OpenAIConfig` defaulting to `openai` / `api.openai.com` keep `developer` by default. Set `compat.supportsDeveloperRole` to override. <!-- publishing-condition: no catalogue generated from this branch or later is published to the slot released binaries read until the site serves by the User-Agent's pig version, or the published copy keeps the explicit false. -->
- CI: the Linux conformance jobs run the extension conformance suite in fourteen shards (seven per job), packed by recorded duration, where eight shards ran 417 to 598 s of go test's 600 s package timeout on CI and a slower runner timed one out. `automation/ci/test-shard-timings.txt` records every top-level test's duration and a fitted cost model; `automation/ci/shard-balance.py pack` writes the shard pins from it and `check` (run by `test/ci-images`) fails when the pins drift from the timings or a shard's predicted time is over 60% of the timeout.
- `cacheWarming` now defaults to `"idle"` instead of `"streaming"`, as in Pi: PiG also keeps eligible prompt caches warm for up to 30 minutes between agent runs, but only when a refresh is expected to pay for itself. Set `"cacheWarming": "streaming"` in the global settings for the previous behavior.
- The `/login` and `/logout` provider lists and the `/login <provider>` completions now show the preferred partners Radius and OpenRouter first, then all other providers alphabetically. In the provider lists, partners are marked with `✦`, the selected Radius row shimmers in the Radius logo colors and the selected OpenRouter row glows in OpenRouter's brand color (lime on dark themes, violet on light themes).
- Rust SDK: the exec function of `BashOperations` (`BashExecFn`) now returns `Result<Option<i64>, BashExecError>`, not `Result<Option<i64>, String>`. `BashExecError` converts from `String` and `&str` (`Err("aborted".into())`, `Err(format!(...).into())`), prints as its message and has `message()`. The error `create_local_bash_operations()` returns for a command that timed out after its shell had exited keeps the shell's exit code and run time in a private field, so a bash tool built on it says `The shell exited with code C after S seconds, but background processes it started kept writing output until the timeout.` also when the operations run on another thread, which the previous release's check by the error string's address did not survive; an error built from its message gives the plain `Command timed out after N seconds`, as in Pi. Update an `exec` closure that returned a `String` error with `.into()`. <!-- fix: d081f54f3a32137447bb4cc8059ad13e8fa25040 -->
- The `ui-views` page and the plugin view carrier doc now state the properties a client puts in the argument of a region's intent (`x`, `y`, `dx`, `dy`, `gesture`, `region`, each only when the intent's declared shape names it) as the approved rule, not a proposal, and say that only the reference web page raises a region gesture: the terminal view client draws no drawings and raises none.
- The `ui-views` page now says what each client draws today: the web page draws grids and drawings and uses `title`, `bindings` and `whenHidden`, and both clients raise a `dismiss` intent. It also says that a web page raises a region's `activate` at the centre of the region when Enter or Space reaches the focused region.
- A Durable commit of a single entry on a local SQLite store costs about twice what it did, because the statements are now Pi's (`INSERT … SELECT json_extract(…) FROM json_each(?)`, one call for any number of batches): 65 µs to 142 µs for one entry, while a call of 100 entries allocates 35% less. The statements are kept identical to Pi's, so the cost is SQLite's to execute them.
- Durable storage on SQLite does less Go work per read and per commit. The native connection is driven through modernc.org/sqlite's own driver connection instead of `database/sql` (one dedicated connection needs no pool, argument conversion or row scanning), a record read decodes the row's text where it is read instead of building a map per row and copying the text, an entry record decodes through its own single-pass decoder without the generic decoder's validation scan first, and the serial operation queue allocates nothing when no operation waits. On the storage benchmark's SQLite reads (n=12, same host, pinned) the geometric mean is 28% faster (an exact entry lookup 40%, an entry page scan 56%, the fork-depth head lookup 31%, a document replay 23 to 27%), with 29% fewer allocations and 43% fewer bytes per read; a commit allocates 11 to 17% less and its time is unchanged within the noise of the host. Statements, pragmas, stored rows and every query result are unchanged.
- Durable storage on SQLite allocates less per commit. An entry record is written as JSON.stringify text in one pass (`EntryRecord.AppendStringify`: the members of `MarshalJSON` appended in place, the same text, with `MarshalJSON` kept for every value the writer does not know), into a pooled buffer that every stored value of a commit shares, and the JSON array parameters of a commit's key reads and deletions are appended to one buffer instead of a string per key. On the storage benchmark's SQLite commits, against the same branch without this change (n=10, same host, pinned): a 100-entry commit 19% faster warm (1.40 to 1.14 ms) and 26% faster fresh, with 33% fewer allocations (2,744 to 1,838) and 32% less memory (264 to 180 KiB) per commit; one entry 8% faster warm, a mixed entry/task/submission/document commit 6%. Reads, which this does not touch, are unchanged, and so are the ten-turn session replays of the durable-bench workload (250 and 1,000 turns, one core and sixteen: within noise).
- Durable storage on SQLite opens its connection in SQLite's multi-thread mode (`SQLITE_OPEN_NOMUTEX`) instead of the serialized mode modernc.org/sqlite hard-codes, so SQLite no longer takes its per-connection mutex on every call. The connection was already used by one goroutine at a time (the serial operation queue holds every operation, `Close` included); a test now enforces that on the real driver connection. modernc.org/sqlite's driver layer is vendored in `third_party/sqlite` with a `_threading_mode` DSN parameter until the same parameter is available upstream. On the storage benchmark's SQLite rows (n=12 interleaved runs, same host, pinned) the geometric mean is 8.3% faster: the document replay and historical reads 11 to 27% (p<=0.024), no row slower, allocations and bytes unchanged, commits unchanged.
- The native SQLite engine is now modernc.org/sqlite v1.62.0 (SQLite 3.54.1, with modernc.org/libc v1.80.1 and memory v1.12.1). A Durable commit on SQLite storage is 28 to 41% faster (one entry 112 to 66 us, 100 entries 3.49 to 2.50 ms, a mixed entry 425 to 299 us, warm; a fresh store's first commit 22 to 26% faster) and opening a store is 31% faster; reads are unchanged or faster (the filtered task scan 18%, an exact document address 7%). Allocation counts are equal and bytes per operation grow by at most 3%. Statements, pragmas and rows are unchanged.
- A prepared SQLite statement keeps one compiled copy per pattern of 0 and 1 parameters it is run with. SQLite 3.54 plans a statement again whenever a bound integer moves between 0 or 1 and any other value, and Durable's fork-depth head lookup binds the root conversation (id 1) at the end of every walk and a deeper one at the start of the next, which made that read 18% slower on the new engine; it is now 7% faster than before the upgrade.
- Go: `harness.RunEndTask`, `RunEndTasks`, and `RunEndTaskOf` are `HookTask`, `HookTasks`, and `HookTaskOf`; `GenerationHooks.AfterTools` returns `(*HookTasks, error)` and `OnYield` returns a `YieldResult` (`*YieldContinue` or `*YieldTasks`). `ToolExecutionApi.CreateTaskErased` and `durable.ToolCreateTask` take `ToolTaskOptions`. `TaskState.Until`, `TaskInspectionState.Until`, and `TaskGraphState.Until` are optional. `durationMs` of a tool result is the span from the tool task's first run (`StartedAt`) to its result on the Harness clock, parks, downtime, and reruns included; a record written before `StartedAt` existed keeps the old measure. `pi.tool` is version 4 and `pi.generation` version 3: a database written by this version is not meant to be opened by an older Harness. The Durable core backend (`durable/core`) stays at its contract pin (the pin e7a0df27) and refuses the new members with `driver.ErrSuspendableWorkNotInCorePin`.
- Durable's SQLite storage inserts every row through bound multi-row `VALUES` statements (1, 2, 4 ... rows, at most 100 parameters each) instead of one JSON array read through `json_each`, so SQLite no longer parses and extracts each row it is given. The stored rows of up to 8 KiB of text are identical to the ones Pi's statement stores, in the same storage classes, with the same errors (larger rows were bound already and are unchanged; a lone surrogate in one is stored raw where Pi stores U+FFFD, as before this change) (a differential test compares every table over random batches: NULLs, Unicode, ill-formed UTF-8, lone surrogates, integer edges and the 8 KiB boundary). Warm commits take 10 to 38% less time and make 11 to 31% fewer allocations (one entry 72 to 57 us, 100 entries 2.4 to 1.5 ms, mixed entry/task/submission/document 305 to 272 us); the first commit of 100 entries takes 34 to 42% less; reads are unchanged, and reopening a storage allocates 12% less.
- An extension that subscribes to `context`, `turn_end` or `agent_end` costs less in a long session, in every mode and every SDK, with the same events and the same bytes on the wire: the host encoded every message of the conversation again for each model request's `context` event and now encodes only the messages that are new since the request before (a 150-message conversation: 7.4 ms and 1,648 allocations became 0.16 ms and 5), the encoder's compaction of a message's JSON crosses string text eight bytes at a time (200 to 970 MB/s), and a fused extension decodes the events the host just encoded without a second validity pass (-27% of the decode). A Bolt `-p` run of 50 tool turns with a plan-mode-style subscriber: a fused Go extension takes 40% less time (6.2 s to 3.7 s), packed and isolated Go extensions 25% less (7.5 s to 5.6 s), a Python subscriber 27% and a Node subscriber 17% less; the cost still grows with the length of the session. <!-- fix: c8d42f6c4 -->
- Extension events cost the host far fewer allocations. One streamed `message_update` handed to a subscribing TypeScript extension now costs 122 allocations and 23.9 KB at one subscriber (381 and 41.1 KB before) and 55 and 9.0 KB per subscriber at four (202 and 26.1 KB before), because the host no longer rebuilds the run's system prompt and options, or spells the request ID and makes the response channel anew, for every delta. An RPC turn with ten extensions costs 4,613 allocations and 731 KB (5,927 and 1.39 MB before). Observable behavior, the wire protocol and every SDK are unchanged.
- An interactive start holds about 96 KB less live heap at the first frame (2.112 MB to 2.016 MB in the process gate, which runs pig in a directory whose AGENTS.md is 62 KB), and builds the system prompt once instead of twice. The three search, paste and tool-pattern caches no longer allocate their maps before the first expression is stored (26 KB), and the system prompt text and its sections now share one copy of the prompt instead of holding two (69 KB with a 62 KB project context file). The prompt text, its sections and the cache limits are unchanged.
- Google providers: `StreamOptions.Fetch` now reaches the `google-generative-ai` and `google-vertex` adapters (API key and Application Default Credentials) instead of failing with `Custom fetch is not supported`; Vertex's ADC token request still uses its own HTTP client. A `CONTINUATION` finish reason ends the turn with stop reason `length`, like `MAX_TOKENS`. <!-- fix: f72f799a4c -->
- Chord telemetry ingest: `telemetryingest.IngestOptions` takes `Admit`, which decides whose pages may send spans; a page of a refused principal fails `forbidden` (`chord.telemetry.page: not admitted`) and nothing it sends is written. The Chord app kit admits every signed-in page. <!-- feat: 7ae9ff8c7b -->
- The Qwen Token Plan providers use the current gateways (`token-plan.maas.qwencloudapi.com` international, `token-plan.maas.qianwenaiapi.com` China), and `qwen-token-plan` and `qwen-token-plan-cn` are named "Qwen Token Plan Team" and "Qwen Token Plan Team CN". Provider ids are unchanged, and a `models.json` override that names an old `aliyuncs.com` host keeps working. <!-- fix: 1397070024 -->
- The find tool's path patterns are relative to the search directory, like grep's `glob`: `src/*.ts` finds `src/a.ts` but no longer `pkg/src/a.ts`; use `**/src/*.ts` to match at any depth. Patterns without `/` still match file names at any depth (Pi #12116).
- The resume command printed on exit is now on its own line after `To resume this session:`, so it can be selected with a triple-click (Pi #12237).
- `openai-completions` requests with no tools no longer send `"tools": []` when the conversation contains tool calls or tool results; some servers (vLLM 0.20+) rejected the empty array. Set `compat.requiresToolsWithToolHistory` for a proxy that needs it. <!-- fix: 7dd0dc1be1 -->
- The OpenAI Codex provider is named `OpenAI Codex`, without the `(legacy)` marker. <!-- fix: c3a48aa340 -->
- Azure's GPT-6 models (`gpt-6-astra`, `gpt-6-luna`, `gpt-6-sol`, `gpt-6.1-sol`, `gpt-6.1-terra`) use Azure Foundry's 1,050,000-token context window. <!-- fix: c3a48aa340 -->
- An extension overlay shows its blocked status, a reset removes every extension overlay, and `ctrl+o` expands the output of a `!` command that is still pending while the agent works. Pending bash output stays in the pending area when a message is queued and moves into the chat when the run settles.
- The model selector and the Hugging Face model search keep the row you browsed to when the catalog refreshes or a search lands, as Pi main does.
- Consecutive cache warming notices merge into one line instead of stacking.
- **Breaking (Go API):** `(*Extension).MarkdownTransformer` takes the new variadic `...sdk.MarkdownTransformerOptions` after the transformer, as Pi's `registerMarkdownTransformer` takes its options. Before: `func(MarkdownTransformerFunc)`. After: `func(MarkdownTransformerFunc, ...MarkdownTransformerOptions)`. A call `ext.MarkdownTransformer(fn)` compiles unchanged and keeps the default surfaces; only a use of the method as a value (a variable, a field or an interface method with the old one-parameter signature) fails to compile. `pig upgrade` names such a use and the new signature.
- The plan-mode example tracks progress more tolerantly, as Pi's does: `[DONE: 1]`, `[DONE 1]`, `Done: 1` and "Step 1 done / is complete / finished" mark a step (never "Step 9 is not done"), thinking blocks count, only the last `Plan:` section is read, step text is no longer cut at 50 characters (the widget shortens it for display), steps that start with a backtick are kept, the widget refreshes every turn, "All steps complete" finishes the plan, and the plan-complete card waits for the next prompt instead of starting a turn.
- chord: the vendored client tree (`chord/nextnode/surfaces/client`) is made from a derived Pi tree, the pin plus Pi 22fe46c7b, 3c771bd18 and da44c4df3 cherry-picked (manifest `carried`, `PI_CARRIED` of the vendoring script), until Pi's chord events (8d30e6306) are carried and the whole closure is re-vendored at a later commit.
- chord: the remote references of one host with one sharing key (type, version, fingerprint, params, placed address, the caller's principal and incarnation) share ONE wire hold: the provider sees one `hold`, and one `release` when the last reference lets go; a reference that lets go earlier sends `abort` for its own sent calls (newest first) and nothing else. `self.get` references, references on a suspended route address and references made after a refusal over the link hold on their own, as before; after `too_large/part` each reference's `retry` moves it alone to a hold of its own. `chord.hold` is a root span on the host's adapter, linked to its first getter (Pi 47e9d74f9, 90ed3e3b1). <!-- feat: 3f059cf1ab -->
- Chord hosts that run Pi's TypeScript (a plugin's Node subprocess, a page, the terminal client) follow Pi main 47e9d74f9 and 90ed3e3b1: the remote references of one host with the same type, version, params, placed address and caller share one hold over a link. A second reference joins it with no message, the last release sends `release`, and releasing one of several cancels only its own calls. A hold's `chord.hold` span is now a root span of the host's telemetry, linked to the span of its first getter, so an exporter sees it outside the getter's trace.
- docs: the Chord tutorial (`docs/chord/tutorial.md`) shows the traces `examples/chord-todo` prints now that the references of one host share one wire hold: in the trap "a trace starts where a span starts" the server's hold of the list is shared work, a `chord.hold` root of its own linked to the request, so the trace of the request (step 11, and the refused request) no longer lists it or the worker's relay of it, and the listed `chord.http` traces count 6 spans (were 8).
- Chord hosts that run Pi's TypeScript (a plugin's Node subprocess, a page, the terminal client) follow Pi 6268cc5cd and 7ae9ff8c7: a plugin of the Node host that opens a store of its own (`openStore` of the Chord API) has `store.onCommitted(listener, onError)`, which announces the last sequence number once the commits it covers are durable; and the vendored telemetry ingest facet takes `admit(principal)`, as the Go facet does. No shipped page or terminal bundle changes.
- After this upgrade every browser and every paired device of an app built with the Chord app kit signs in again. The kit's sessions are now sign-ins (Pi ff7414d51, "Sign-ins, not sessions"), under new names with no alias and no migration, as in Pi: nothing stored or held under the old names is read. The old stored document stays in the server's store untouched; a browser with the old cookie gets 401 (no redirect: open the owner link the start prints); a paired device's token gets 401 (pair it again); the owner token file is replaced at the next start, so command-line clients on the same machine keep working.
- Chord app kit, renamed on the wire and in the store: the contract and core facet `chord.app.sessions` -> `chord.app.sign-ins`; the stored document `chord.app.sessions` with the field `sessions` -> `chord.app.sign-ins` with the field `signIns`; the cookie `chord-session` -> `chord-sign-in`.
- Chord app kit, renamed start option: `AppLimits.EphemeralSessions` -> `AppLimits.EphemeralSignIns` (Pi `limits.ephemeralSessions` -> `limits.ephemeralSignIns`).
- Chord app kit, renamed: `app.Sessions` -> `app.SignIns`.
- Chord app kit, renamed: `app.SessionInfo` -> `app.SignInInfo`.
- Chord app kit, renamed: `app.SessionKind` -> `app.SignInKind`, with `SessionBrowser`, `SessionDevice`, `SessionEphemeral` -> `SignInBrowser`, `SignInDevice`, `SignInEphemeral`.
- Chord app kit, renamed: `app.SessionCookie` -> `app.SignInCookie`.
- Chord app kit, renamed: `app.SessionLimits` -> `app.SignInLimits`.
- Chord app kit, renamed: `app.KitSessions` -> `app.KitSignIns`.
- Chord app kit, renamed: `app.CreateSessions` -> `app.CreateSignIns`.
- Chord app kit, renamed: `app.EphemeralSessions` -> `app.EphemeralSignIns`, `app.NewEphemeralSessions` -> `app.NewEphemeralSignIns`.
- chord: a client and a page can set the limits per part of what arrives from the server (Pi 34fb59f67). `surfaces.ClientOptions.Limits` (`*link.PartLimits`: `Part` bytes on the wire, `Decoded` bytes after inflating) and the page's `limits` option take them; without them a client keeps an untrusted link's limits, 16 MiB on the wire and 64 MiB decoded. A part past a limit fails as on any link with limits: a client that cannot take the scripts object's set keeps the code it started with.
- ai: Mistral tool definitions are now sent non-strict by default. A Mistral model receives its tools with `strict: false` and the schema as the tool declares it unless its `compat.supportsStrictMode` is `true`; before, every tool that asked for JSON-schema constrained sampling went out `strict: true` with a converted schema (`additionalProperties: false`, every property required). The new `supportsStrictMode` member (default `false`) of the Mistral compat in `models.json` turns strict tools back on for a model or a Mistral-compatible provider that handles them; a tool that requires strict sampling (`strict: "require"`) now fails before any request, with `Tool "<name>" requires JSON-schema constrained sampling, but strict tools are unsupported.`, on a model without the flag (Pi 2c2a77f9f3ab, #12148). Follows Pi 2c2a77f9f3ab and 2145e3f6099c.
- Follows Pi ac78a6068b38 (#12117, #11264): a changelog that exists but cannot be read (an extension package's `CHANGELOG.md` that is a directory, say) gives no startup notes and no `/changelog` entries, and nothing is written over the interactive screen. PiG's own code already did this (it returns no entries at the failed read and the bundled changelog is embedded, so `/changelog` shows `No changelog entries found.`); the change is the Node extension runtime's copy of Pi's changelog reader and the parity oracle, which no longer print `Warning: Could not parse changelog` there. Pi's unused `restoreModelFromSession`, which printed model-restore messages, has no PiG counterpart and nothing is removed.
- Follows Pi c8c456c85c6e (#12234): with no model at all (no login, no `models.json` model) the `No models available. Use /login ...` guidance is now also a warning in the runtime diagnostics, so print, JSON and RPC mode write `Warning: No models available. ...` to stderr once, before the missing-key error that print and JSON mode already print, and RPC mode once at startup (not again after `switch_session` or `fork`). Pi's changelog line does not say this; it is what Pi itself does, measured: its model is never undefined (the agent starts with a placeholder model), so the commit's "unchanged" for this case does not hold. Interactive mode shows the guidance once, as before. The same warning is also listed by the other ways a start ends without a model: after the error of `--provider <name>` without `--model` (or of an unknown `--model`, or `--api-key` without a model), and before the output of `--help` and `--list-models`.
- Fullscreen scroll frames reuse the previous frame's component output: the wheel, page and line keys, top and bottom, prompt jumps, scrollbar drag and selection auto-scroll request a view-only frame, and Container.Render and Box.Render return the same slice while their children's lines are unchanged. Follows Pi b7bb7ca905b8. Breaking for in-process Go components: the slice a Container or Box returns is borrowed and read-only; copy it (slices.Clone) before changing a line, also in a type that embeds a Container and edits its own Render result; its capacity equals its length, so append is safe. Known limit, as in Pi: a component that changes state without requesting a render stays stale while scrolling (it was already stale without scrolling). A Node extension gets Pi's rule exactly once the backport is vendored: "Extension components: `render()` now returns `readonly string[]`, and `Container` returns the same cached array while its children are unchanged. Extensions that modify render output in place, including `super.render()` in a `Container` subclass or an embedded component's output, must copy it first".. The SDKs that push lines (Python, Rust, Lisp, subprocess) pass lines by value and are unaffected.
- Follows Pi b513b64d8ac8: at interactive startup, installing a missing git or npm package no longer prints the output of git and npm (`Cloning into ...`, npm summaries and lifecycle script output) before the screen; a successful install shows only `Installing <source>...` and a failed command reports the last 8000 characters of its output. A git package whose remote needs a typed password or ssh passphrase no longer prompts there: git is run with `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` (and ssh with `BatchMode=yes` unless `GIT_SSH_COMMAND` is set), so the install fails with a hint to set up a git credential helper or an ssh agent, or to run `pig install <source>` once from the shell. Credential helpers and ssh agents keep working. `pig install`, `pig update` and the print, JSON and RPC modes are unchanged: they keep git and npm output on the terminal.
- Follows Pi e56d35ce5ece: the default model for the `openai`, `azure` and `openai-codex` providers is now GPT-6.2 Sol (`gpt-6.2-sol`) instead of GPT-6.1 Sol, at the same price.
- Follows Pi cead615b48b8: the OpenAI Codex provider lists GPT-6.2 Sol with a 500K context window (it was 272K in the first GPT-6.2 listing); GPT-6.2 Astra keeps 272K. These are the defaults Codex's own model list returns.
- durable/codemode: code mode namespaces come from extensions, not name prefixes (Pi 5e24c6b1f). An extension declares one with `durable.Extension.Namespace` (`durable.ToolNamespace{Name, Description, Instructions}`) and it groups the tools the extension brings; a tool several extensions name belongs to the first one's. `codemode.Namespace`, its `Prefix`, `codemode.ToolOptions.Namespaces` and the unexported `namespaceOf` are removed with no replacement for prefixes: declare the namespace on the extension that brings the tools (for example one extension per MCP server) and use the plain tool names. `Section` takes the selected extensions instead of namespaces (`Section(tools, extensions, budget)`) and `codemode.NamespacesOf(extensions)` maps tool names to their namespaces. The `codemode` prompt section now lists the ungrouped tools first, then every namespace a selected extension declares, also one without tools yet, as `## <name>` and its one-line description with no tool counts (`(some tools not listed)` and `(tools not listed)` are gone; a single `Some tools are not listed: find them with searchTools().` line follows the heading line), so the prompt does not change when an extension's deferred tools appear. `Instructions` are returned only by `describeNamespace()`, and `searchTools()` searches the name, description and instructions. The start data of a code mode call lists a declared namespace without tools too, and always carries its description. The coding agent's own code mode and the extension SDKs are not changed.
- Interactive mode keeps one `message_update` for each part of the message while it collects the events that Pi's event loop handles in one task, where it kept every update until the task ended: a response that arrives in one piece no longer holds hundreds of partial messages or sets the message block hundreds of times for one frame. A chunk of a response that streams, which is a task of one `message_update`, reaches the screen loop as one event again instead of one event between two task markers. With both, drawing a reply and the end of its run in one frame costs no CPU: a prompt of a long session takes 2 % to 3 % fewer user instructions than before that fix, where the fix alone took 3 % more, and a streamed response takes as many as before it.
- Fullscreen scroll frames reuse the previous frame's component output (Pi b7bb7ca905b8, [#9549](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/9549)): the wheel, page and line keys, top and bottom, prompt jumps, scrollbar drag and selection auto-scroll request a view-only frame, `Container.Render` and `Box.Render` return the same slice while their children's lines are unchanged, and a mouse event finds its child by the cached child heights without copying. The cost of a wheel frame no longer grows with the length of the transcript.
- An interactive run keeps a heap goal of at least 16 MiB (D621): after each collection it collects next at the larger of 16 MiB and the goal of its GC percent, which stays 150 until more than 8 MiB of heap is live and is 100 from then on, also when the heap has shrunk again. On the fake-model benchmark the interactive scenario's CPU falls about 7 % and its time to interactive 12 %, a session of five prompts runs 14.5 % fewer user instructions, and a long session 1.6 to 3.2 % fewer user instructions per prompt; the interactive scenario's peak own memory rises from 16.8 to 20.2 MB and an idle session keeps about 1.1 MB more Go memory. `GOGC` or `GOMEMLIMIT` in the environment turn the policy off as before. <!-- change: ebe5b873cc28d93a7548e8d5d65280a190a1d1c9 -->
- A plugin UI registry holds at most 8 attachments, clients of every kind together; a further `Registry.Attach` fails with `limit`.
- `uiview.Registry.Subscribe` is replaced by `Registry.Attach`, and `UIBridge.SetClientAbilities` returns an error for abilities outside the record. Neither was in a release, so no migration is needed.
- A program that embeds PiG and draws no extension mount in a terminal no longer links the terminal's image drawing or Go's JPEG and GIF decoders. The half-block drawing of a mount's image, which the terminal without an image protocol shows, now reads its pixels with the port of Pi's Photon decode (`internal/photonimage`) for every format, PNG included, instead of Go's decoders; a program that draws mount surfaces in its own terminal sets `subprocess.MountImages.Decode`, and without it such an image is one line of text that names the missing decoder and the field.
- **Breaking (Go API):** `coding/extension/host/subprocess`: a program that embeds the extension host and mounts view-kit widgets (`grid`, `input`, `scroll-view`, `mouse-region`, `bordered-loader`, `cancellable-loader`, `branch-summary`, `compaction-summary`, `custom-message` and `skill-invocation`) must now call `subprocess.EnableViewWidgets()` once before the first view is built, as it calls `subprocess.EnableEditorViews()` for editors. The `pig` command calls both before it runs a command, so nothing changes for `pig` or a Piglet Binary. A program that does not call it no longer links the widget builders (the headless example, `examples/sdk`, `pig-evals` and the repository's tools do not), and it rejects a view that holds a widget with an error that names the call: the surface keeps its previous frame, a message or tool renderer's result counts as a failed render, the rejection is reported once per surface through the extension error listeners, and the extension is sent nothing. `EnableViewWidgets` does not link the terminal editor. <!-- fix: 0749ea17ba963df29f9008111518533d00575c88 -->
- A map returned from a `before_provider_headers` handler is now ignored, as in Pi, in the Go, Python, Rust and Lisp extension SDKs, and for a handler an embedding program puts on `extension.Extension.Handlers["before_provider_headers"]` (the typed `extension.API.OnBeforeProviderHeaders` handler has no result to return). The headers a request carries are the ones the handlers leave on `event.headers`: edit `event.headers` in place instead of returning a map, and set a header to `null` to delete it from the request. A returned map replaced the headers in those SDKs from v0.2.0 to v0.7.0, so an extension that returned headers from this handler loses them until it edits `event.headers`; the Node SDK already ignored the return. A `before_provider_request` handler is unchanged: a payload it returns still replaces the request's payload. <!-- fix: 28e26ff6f5d393238e8f80bd41a4f80bcfffeb0e -->
- A provider re-registration with `insecure: false` now turns certificate checks back on for that provider's endpoint. Before, only unregistering the provider did: a re-registration could set `insecure: true` but not undo it, a rule that shipped in 0.5.0 and held through 0.7.0. A re-registration that leaves `insecure` out still keeps the earlier value, as Pi's `registerProvider` keeps any value a re-registration leaves undefined (`model-runtime.ts:970-977`). Every extension SDK says it the same way: the `insecure` member of the provider config, absent, `false` or `true`. The Go extension API keeps `ProviderConfig.Insecure bool` (true is on, the zero value is omitted) and adds `InsecureSetting()` for the three states.
- A provider that `models.json` marks `insecure: true` and an extension registers again now answers one rule on every request route. A registration that states `insecure` wins, `true` or `false`; one that states nothing keeps the file's opt-in only while it keeps the file's endpoint, and one that names its own `baseUrl` verifies certificates at that endpoint. Before, the two routes a request takes disagreed: a request through the model runtime dropped the file's opt-in whenever the provider was registered (since 0.3.0), and a provider built straight from a model entry (`coding.BuildModel`, which the CLI's `--model`, the interactive model picker and an extension's model switch use for a provider without a native stream function) kept the file's opt-in and ignored the registration's, even an explicit `insecure: false` (since 0.2.0).
- Quitting interactive mode (ctrl+d, `/quit`, ctrl+c twice) while an extension's `session_shutdown` handler never settles now ends the way Pi's quit does: PiG waits until no extension holds a timer, an open connection, a child process or a running command, instead of ending at the first extension process that has nothing left to do. PiG runs extensions in several processes, so each Node extension process reports its own idle event loop, and a command of an extension written in Go, Rust, Python or Lisp that is still running holds the quit. A command of such an extension that never returns now holds this quit for ever (it ended at once before), where Pi's process, which has no handle to wait for, exits at once; ctrl+c, SIGINT, SIGTERM and SIGHUP end it at once as in Pi (divergence D650).
- At the stopped terminal of a quit that waits for an extension, SIGTERM and SIGHUP now end PiG at once, with exit status 143 and 129 as in Pi. They did not end it.
- `install.sh` and the npm launcher now say that PiG doesn't run on iPhone, iPad, or iSH, and how to use PiG from such a device (connect with `ssh` to a computer that has PiG installed, then run `pig` there), instead of reporting an unsupported CPU architecture (`iPhone18,3`) or a missing npm package for `ios/arm64`. Both still exit with status 1.
- The ordered-object JSON readers (extension provider headers, login duplicate-field scan, model registry headers, the models store and catalog readers, theme loading, the model generators, `internal/orderedjson`, tool-call argument entries and the parity tools) now read with `encoding/json/jsontext` and the `internal/jsonopts` option set instead of `encoding/json` v1 tokens. They are closer to `JSON.parse` in two ways. A document cut off after a value (`{"a":1`, or `{"a":1]`) is now an error: the readers that returned once they had their keys never checked the closing token. A document that is not an object but an array (`[1]`) is now an error or no entries, where some readers answered with garbage or panicked. A number outside float64 range at the top level is not an error either: `JSON.parse` gives `Infinity` for `1e400`, so a reader that wants an object returns no entries for it, as Pi does. The extension login duplicate-field scan no longer rejects such a number itself; the typed decode that follows still does. Decoding cost and allocations are unchanged within benchmark noise.
- Six readers stay on `encoding/json` v1 on purpose: `ai/auth_store.go`, `ai/credential_json.go`, `coding/cli/rpc_object.go`, `coding/extension/builtin/codemode/execute.go`, `internal/codingagent/session_export.go` and the extension conformance test fixture. They share `extensions/sdk/json`, which keeps a lone surrogate (`"\ud800"`) as WTF-8 bytes the way JavaScript strings do. `jsonopts.Parse` turns invalid UTF-8, and so a WTF-8 lone surrogate, into U+FFFD, which would change a value Pi passes through unchanged.
