- The login duplicate-field fuzz target no longer skips a document with a number outside float64 range: the reference reads numbers as raw tokens like the scan, and both accept `1e999` where `JSON.parse` gives `Infinity` (the typed decode of the definition still rejects it).
- The Go language floor of a generated extension module recognises a release candidate or beta by `go/version` instead of a letter set.
- Building PiG from source needs Go 1.27: the root module's `go` directive (`go.mod` and `go.work`) is now 1.27.0 instead of 1.26.0, because its JSON code moves to `encoding/json/v2` and `encoding/json/jsontext`. `go install github.com/MichaelKinsy/PiG/cmd/pig@latest` with a Go older than 1.27 downloads the toolchain `go.mod` names (Go 1.21 or newer), or fails under `GOTOOLCHAIN=local`. The Porter extension and the extension conformance fixtures, which require the root module, move to 1.27.0 with it. The extension SDK (`extensions/sdk`), the other piglet modules, the examples and the Go extensions `pig extension init` generates keep Go 1.26. `internal/jsonopts` holds the one `encoding/json/v2` option set that follows `JSON.parse` and `JSON.stringify`: duplicate names allowed with the last value winning, invalid UTF-8 replaced with U+FFFD, case-sensitive member names, and no HTML or U+2028/U+2029 escaping on output.
- Faster JSON on the wire (`646e507248`, `f153eff9e8`, `8597e91783`): a Mistral request with 64 messages makes 4 allocations instead of 261 (132 before Go 1.27's engine), marshaling an agent message 16 instead of 34, a command line that carries an image is read in about a ninth of the time, and a host protocol frame in a third to a half. The bytes written match `JSON.stringify`: an agent message or content block that holds a negative zero is written with `0` (it was `-0`) and one that holds an ill-formed UTF-8 byte with the replacement character itself (it was the escape `\ufffd`), from `json.Marshal`, the extension wire and provider request bodies alike, as Pi writes them; nothing else changes. An RPC command line or protocol frame with a lone UTF-16 surrogate (an escape, or its three-byte form), or one that does not decode, is read by the decoder it always was, also when an escaped backslash precedes the text of an escape. One protocol frame difference: a host protocol frame's member names are matched exactly; the old decoder also matched them in another letter case, and the SDKs write the protocol's own spelling.
- Inside tmux, `pig -p` no longer starts `tmux` to learn the color mode: the theme needs only true color, which the hyperlink probe does not decide. A `pig -p` turn in tmux took 9.2 ms and now takes 7.0 ms.
- The default llama.cpp server URL is now `http://127.0.0.1:9931`, the port the current llama.cpp server listens on, as in Pi (#12001): `/llama`, the `llama.cpp` provider and the setup text use it when neither a saved credential nor `LLAMA_BASE_URL` names a server. If you run llama.cpp on port 8080, set `LLAMA_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8080` (or save that URL in the `llama.cpp` credential). The llama.cpp and NVIDIA RTX guides use 9931 and no longer pass `--port 8080`.
- The llama.cpp provider's default server URL is `http://127.0.0.1:9931`, matching llama.cpp's current server default, as in Pi. <!-- fix: cafa121edf -->
- The context estimate counts the arguments of a tool call whose members are ASCII strings (a write or an edit) from their bytes instead of encoding them. A turn of a session that wrote files, with a provider that reports no usage, no longer encodes the text of every earlier write three times: counting the arguments of a 200 KB write takes 0.07 ms instead of 0.48 ms and allocates nothing instead of 238 KB. <!-- change: aadeceec10 -->
- tui: a streaming assistant message keeps the rendered blocks of its last frame across a garbage collection, so the frame after a collection renders only what the new text changed instead of every block of the answer. The rows are unchanged. On a stream of a 20,000-character Markdown answer with a collection every 30 frames, a stream takes 27 % less time and allocates 14 % less.
- tui: highlighting a code block allocates far less and takes about half the time. A match of the highlighter no longer records the capture groups of every rule of its matcher, the words of a mode with keywords are found without a regular expression, and a block that streams converts its code into a reused buffer. The highlighted output is unchanged. Replaying the code blocks of a streamed 20,000-character Markdown answer frame by frame takes 47 % less time, 73 % fewer bytes and 64 % fewer allocations; a stream of that answer with a collection every 30 frames takes 29 % less time and allocates 44 % less.
- tui: a streamed code block that one construct holds open from its first line to its last (a JSON document is one object or one list; a long block comment) is no longer highlighted again from its start at every frame. The highlighter resumes inside the open constructs, a few lines before the end of the block. The highlighted output is unchanged. Replaying a streamed JSON document of 200 lines frame by frame hands the highlighter 1.21 characters for each character of code instead of 10.30, and takes 85 % less time, 87 % fewer bytes and 87 % fewer allocations. Of the 190 languages the highlighter's samples cover, 47 read less text again when they stream, among them css, xml, scala, kotlin, haskell, erlang, clojure, dockerfile, twig and django; the others read what they read before.
- PiG no longer samples heap allocations for profiling unless `PIG_PROFILE` names `heap` or `allocs` or `GODEBUG` sets `memprofilerate` (D627); a heap profile that another tool takes from a default run is empty. It lowers the memory of a session by about 1 to 2 MB (peak memory of the interactive scenario -1.5 MB, resident memory of a 40-prompt session -1.75 MB) and the user instructions of a `-p` run by 0.9 %; CPU time, wall time and time to interactive did not change. <!-- change: 5c0a152a0 -->
- The root module zip that `go install` downloads is about 2.8 MB smaller: the SDK test trees (`extensions/sdk-py/tests`, `extensions/sdk-lisp/tests`, `extensions/sdk-rs/tests`) and the benchmark data trees (`bench/evals`, `bench/bolt-aot`, `bench/compare`, `bench/k8s/image`) now sit in data-only nested modules. The files stay in the repository and are read by path; the `pig` binary is unchanged.
- CI: `make module-pins` (part of `ci-bookkeeping`) now also fails when the root `go.mod` pins the extension SDK at a commit that is not in the history of the branch it runs on: the 12 hex digits of a pseudo-version, or the commit of the tag `extensions/sdk/<version>` (a release or a pre-release such as `v0.8.0-rc.1`), must be an ancestor of `HEAD`. A pin of another line is public and passes `make module-publication` and `make module-size`, then dangles when the branch is squash-merged. A shallow checkout that cannot answer fails with a message that asks for the full history instead of passing.
- `extensions/sdk-py/pig_sdk` and `extensions/sdk-rs/src` are directories with their own `go.mod`, as `extensions/sdk-lisp/src` is, so the root module zip that `go install` downloads is 128.5 MB instead of 132.3 MB (3.8 MB of Python and Rust SDK sources that no Go package embeds or imports). The files stay in the repository; PiG still carries both SDKs in their embedded packs, which are unchanged, and Python, cargo, tests, generators and drift gates read the directories by path.
- The root module zip that `go install` downloads is 131.5 MB instead of 134.2 MB: `changelog.d` joins the data-only directories with their own `go.mod` (the changelog tools accept that one file there).
- Twenty-five more data-only directories (the recorded model catalog source, the test shard timing tables, the recorded oracle data and the fixtures of many tests) have their own `go.mod`, so the root module zip that `go install` downloads is 132.0 MB instead of 134.2 MB. No Go package embeds or imports them; the files stay in the repository and the generators, tests and drift gates read them by path.
- `extensions/sdk-ts`, `extensions/sdk-lisp/src`, `internal/pigdocs/content` and `chord/nextnode/http/testdata` are directories with their own `go.mod`, so the root module zip that `go install` downloads is 130.7 MB instead of 135.3 MB (4.6 MB of TypeScript declarations, Common Lisp sources, docs pages and recorded URL corpora that no Go package embeds or imports). The files stay in the repository; PiG still carries the Lisp SDK and the docs in their embedded packs, and npm, ASDF, tests, generators and drift gates read the directories by path.
- CI: the nightly workflow's race and allocation jobs prepare the pinned Pi oracle with `make upstream-mirror`, the step `ci.yml`'s Linux job runs, so the Pi-oracle tests find the npm trees they import from (`durable/interop`, `internal/typebox/testdata/npm`, `ai/testdata/sdk`) and the two workflows cannot list different installs; the race job installs the pinned SBCL as `ci.yml` does, which `cmd/pig`'s Lisp SDK test needs. The agent, ai, libs and rest shards failed every night with `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, and cli shard 4/4 with `sbcl is required`.
- CI: the nightly fuzz job's timeout is 60 minutes, not 30: the 47 targets take 41 s each (30 s of fuzzing, 11 s of build and corpus work), so the job was cancelled at the 41st on 2026-11-05, 11-06 and 11-08 and the last targets were never fuzzed. A test fails when targets are added past what the timeout covers.
- CI: `FuzzMarkdownRenderStaysWithinWidth` allows the one row Pi's Markdown emits wider than the width, a double-width character at width 1 (`breakLongWord` appends a grapheme to a fresh row whatever its width); every other wider row still fails.
- The allocation benchmarks that start a program (`BenchmarkClipboardImageCommand`, `BenchmarkNpmMetadataLookup`, `BenchmarkPackageInheritedOutput`) run with `PATH` alone, and `BenchmarkClipboardImageCommand` reads no `binfmt_misc` handlers (every spawn reads each one the machine registers, about 14 allocations each), so their allocs/op no longer follow the variables, the `PATH` and the kernel registrations of the machine that runs them; `BenchmarkAutocompleteCommandOrder` runs with a one-directory `PATH`.
- The allocation baseline lowers 32 entries that the code had improved on, adds the 23 benchmarks it had no entry for, and lowers `BenchmarkSessionClone` from 26213 to 25710 allocs/op: `/fork` of a file-backed session streams the branch to the clone's file and opens that file as a resume does, which holds a 427 MB session's peak at Pi's level, and the per-line allocations of the index load that costs are cut at the source.
- Starting a Node extension for the first time in a process extracts the embedded runtime with one directory step per directory (213) instead of one per file (1871), and the hash of a Go module's sources reads each `.go` file once instead of twice. The extracted tree (paths, bytes, modes) and the digest of `extensions/sdk` are unchanged. On the benchmark rows, allocations per extraction fell from 38,612 to 35,309 (8.6 % fewer, 3 of 3 runs each) and the 16-extension Go content-hash row from 63,678 to 63,421.
- A start no longer builds OpenRouter's 806 `:nitro` and `:floor` routing variants to resolve the model. `--model`, the default model and the SDK's model resolution read a listing of ids and names (0.12 MB) instead of the variant entries (0.81 MB); a variant is built when it is selected or when a model list is shown. Live heap at ready: interactive 2.78 MB to 2.07 MB, `-p` 2.38 MB to 1.61 MB, `--mode rpc` 2.16 MB to 1.45 MB, and 0.56 MB less is allocated per start. A start with an OpenRouter key or with a Node extension still builds the variants, since it lists every model. What `--model` resolves to, the model lists and the `--list-models` output are unchanged.
- PiG holds each OpenRouter `:nitro` and `:floor` routing variant once. A variant was kept twice once a model list had been read (at a start with `--model`, in the model selector, by `--list-models`): as an entry of its own and as a copy in the list. The list is now the one place a variant is held, and a lookup returns the list's entry: 0.32 MB less live heap after the list is read (2,531,608 to 2,212,648 bytes, 803 fewer objects). The model lists, every lookup and the `--list-models` output are unchanged.
- Google providers: the request payload a `before_provider_request` handler (`StreamOptions.OnPayload`) receives for `google-generative-ai` and `google-vertex` now carries `config.automaticContinuation: false`, as Pi's does since f72f799a4 (#12103). It is an option of Pi's Google SDK and is not sent in the request body. The body's member order follows `@google/genai` 2.32.0, the SDK version that commit moves Pi to: on Vertex a `functionResponse` is written as `id`, `name`, `parts`, `response`; on the Gemini API `inlineData` and `fileData` keep the member order of the payload (`mimeType` before `data` for PiG's own image parts); and a replaced payload's `labels`, `continuationToken` and `store` (Gemini API) or `continuationToken` and `generationOutputConfig` (Vertex, sent as `outputConfig`) and a part's `speechMetadata` are sent.
- `third_party/pi-packs`, the vendored npm packs of the pinned Pi build, is a data-only directory with its own `go.mod`, so the root module zip that `go install` downloads is 132.8 MB again instead of 138.2 MB (5.4 MB of tarballs that no Go package embeds or imports). The packs stay in the repository; the `file:` dependencies, `automation/pin` and `internal/pioracle` read them by path.
- Resuming a long session holds far less memory and a turn no longer does work proportional to the session's length: a loaded session keeps about 79 bytes per JSONL line (it was 106), its ids live in one arena instead of one string each, and the active branch and the context messages are cached and extended on append, so a turn allocates the same at turn 50 as at turn 3,500. Session files and every observable session, tree, branch and compaction result are unchanged.
- Startup refreshes the built-in provider catalogs with fewer allocations: one file-read snapshot lookup and one value-only parent context per refresh instead of one per credential and models-store read of each of the 168 providers, one job object per provider instead of five closures, and no per-signal method value or publication closure. RPC start (`process.rpc_startup`) falls from 13,416 to 12,460 allocations and 1.81 MB to 1.77 MB; print mode (`process.print`) from 15,527 to 14,732 allocations and 2.12 MB to 2.10 MB (go1.27.4, GOMAXPROCS=1, test/perfgate). The ceilings move down to 13,000 / 1.85 MB and 15,300 / 2.2 MB. Output and behavior are unchanged.
- When both `PIG_TELEMETRY` and `PI_TELEMETRY` are set, `PIG_TELEMETRY` now decides. Before, `PI_TELEMETRY` did.
- The `pig-acp` release archives are built from `@pi-in-go/pigpen-acp` 0.2.2, so `pig-acp --version` reports 0.2.2 and a relative `--pig` such as `./pig` resolves against the directory of `pig-acp`, not the session working directory, and without `--pig` the `pig` beside `pig-acp` is used before any `pig` on `PATH`; a registry entry that starts `./pig-acp` finds the `pig` of its archive.
- The `pig-acp-<version>-<os>-<arch>` archives are flat: `pig-acp` and `pig` sit at the archive root, not under a versioned `pig-acp-<version>-<os>-<arch>/` directory, so the ACP registry entry's fixed `cmd` (`./pig-acp`, `./pig-acp.exe` on Windows) stays valid at every release. Extract them into a directory of your choosing.
- The `pig-acp` release archives are built from `@pi-in-go/pigpen-acp` 0.2.3, so `pig-acp --version` reports 0.2.3 (ACP-AUTH-002).
- The default budget of `pig-bolt`'s compiled images is 2 GB (was 1 GB): one image is 240 to 270 MB, so 1 GB held three or four sets and each eviction cost a 20 to 30 s background rebuild. `/bolt-runtime budget` and `PIG_AOT_CACHE_MAX` still set it.
- On Linux a slot TypeScript runtime now runs the file PiG verified: the check keeps the executable open and starts it as `/proc/self/fd/N`, so replacing the path after the check changes nothing that runs (`ps` shows the descriptor number as the process name; `/proc/<pid>/exe` and the command line name the path). The start-check record is no longer read through a symlink or a FIFO, and a file written within two seconds of its hash starting is not recorded. Other platforms start the executable by path.
- A start that selects a slot TypeScript runtime no longer re-hashes an unchanged executable. A passing SHA-256 check is recorded next to the executable, keyed by device, inode, size, modification time and status-change time, and skipped while all of them and the manifest's digest are unchanged. The digest comparison, the Bun lock check and the `--version` probe still run at every start. For a 233 MiB compiled host the digest and probe step fell from about 290 to 370 ms to about 2 to 4 ms on a second start in a new process.
- MCP OAuth `clientRegistration: "cimd"` now identifies PiG with its Client ID Metadata Document on PiG's own origin, `https://pi-in-go.dev/oauth/client.json` (or `https://pi-in-go.dev/oauth/<id>/client.json` with `/callback/<id>`), in the Go host and the Node runtime. Pi's own build uses `https://pi.dev/oauth/…`; nothing else differs.
- A Markdown component keeps the wraps, inline renderings, highlighted code and resume point of a streamed render only through a weak pointer, as Pi's `markdown.ts` holds its rendered blocks in a `WeakRef`: a garbage collection releases them and the next render rebuilds them, with the same rows.
- Listing the available models builds the catalog of a Radius provider only when the provider has auth: with no Radius credential it no longer clones and rebuilds every Radius model to discard them, which cost about 550 of the 910 allocations of one call with a Copilot account (364 after, measured at `-benchtime=5x`; the catalog grew with the Pi pin follow (f8f335a21) and took the call to 1002-1056). The `BenchmarkCopilotAccountAvailability` baseline in `automation/ci/allocbase` is lowered to 364.
- Reading the full model catalog and rebuilding the request-auth runtime no longer build the bundled Radius catalog only to replace it, and the Radius baseline is no longer copied a second time at construction: `BenchmarkRuntimeModelsSelection` 811 to 604 and `BenchmarkRequestAuthProviderProjection` 815 to 599 allocations per call (`-benchtime=200x`; the gate baselines are lowered to the measured 595 and 598).
- CI: the nightly fuzz job's timeout is 90 minutes: the tree has 111 fuzz targets, each taking 45 s (30 s of fuzzing and 15 s of build and corpus work), and the job's checkout, Go setup and first build take 5 minutes, which is 111 x 45 s + 5 min = 88 minutes. `test/ci-images/nightly_fuzz_budget_test.go` fails when targets are added past what the timeout covers.
- A warm start with a Node extension loads the extension runtime's own modules from Node's native bytecode cache instead of compiling them from source: `<config-root>/cache/node-compile` is now activated at process start once an earlier run has created it (the first start still activates it at the first SDK import, so a cold start serializes neither the runtime nor Jiti's Babel). A start with one package extension that imports `pi-ai` and `pi-tui` is about 16 ms faster with warm caches (430 to 414 ms median, 32 paired runs on reserved cores, Pi 406 ms); the TypeScript-file and cold-cache starts are unchanged. `NODE_DISABLE_COMPILE_CACHE=1` still disables the cache.
- Go: `chord/sqlite/node` and `durable/storage/sqlite/node` take Pi's `mode` as `NodeSqliteDatabaseOptions.Mode` (`NodeSqliteReadWrite`, `NodeSqliteReadOnly`) and as the second argument of `NewNodeSqliteDatabase`, replacing the `ReadOnly` option; an empty mode is read-write as before. `durable.CompactionOverrides.Get` returns the override and whether the model has an entry, as indexing Pi's `modelOverrides` object does. A read-only connection and the compaction settings behave as before.
- Streaming a provider response costs fewer allocations per delta record, with the same events in the same order. Marginal allocations per frame through the HTTP client, decoder, builder and event stream (measured on linux/amd64, go1.27.4, TestStreamFrameAllocationCeilings): openai-completions text 12.1 to 8.1 and tool-call arguments 22.2 to 18.2, openai-responses text 13.1 to 9.1, anthropic text 18.1 to 9.1 and tool-call arguments 28.2 to 19.2, Google text 69.0 to 26.2, Mistral text 38.3 to 21.2, openai-codex-responses text 33.1 to 29.2. Bytes per frame fall for every provider (Google 3,040 to 1,920, Mistral 3,043 to 1,518) and the ceilings in `automation/perf/ratchet.toml` drop to match.
- An abort (Esc, or the abort of a quit) while a `tool_call`, `tool_result` or `context` extension handler runs no longer abandons the handler: as in Pi, the run waits for it and goes on with its result, and the extension sees the abort as `ctx.signal`. A handler that waits (a confirmation, a timer) should watch `ctx.signal`; the abort and the quit wait for a handler that does not. A handler whose extension process ends while it is awaited fails with the connection's error and the run ends.
- A Node extension handler for `turn_end`, `agent_end`, `message_end`, `tool_call`, `tool_result` or `context`, or a tool's `execute`, that awaits a promise that never settles and holds no timer or I/O no longer keeps a quit waiting after RPC input ended: the process exits when its event loop is empty, as Pi's does (15 ms in Pi 1.5.2; the quit held for ever, or for the 3 s tool abort grace).
- The interactive quit (Ctrl+D, Ctrl+C twice, `/quit`) in the settle tail of a run no longer waits for the run's `agent_settled` handlers: the Session is idle then, and Pi's dispose, which awaits the idle Session, goes on to `session_shutdown` at once (a handler on a 3 s timer held the quit for 2.4 s here, 94 ms in Pi). A quit while a run is still streaming still waits for the run and its `agent_settled` handlers, as Pi does.
- The README names Common Lisp among the extension languages, lists every extension SDK directory and each language's toolchain, states that TypeScript extensions need Node.js 22.13 or newer, and dates the `pig --version` change as new in 0.8.0 (0.7.0 prints `0.7.0+1.5.0`). It describes PiG Standard's four extensions and the SBCL requirement for `make check`, and its version-check commands use `pig version`, which prints the same in 0.7.0 and 0.8.0. It documents `pig --mode rpc --listen` (D232) as new in 0.8.0.
- The `pig` binary is about 0.16 MB smaller: the embedded QuickJS module of `codemode` is stored as a zstd frame (260 KB instead of 287 KB), and the fuzzy filter of the selectors and the autocomplete (`FuzzyFilter`) and the keybinding conflict list no longer compile a copy of the sort for each element type they sort. The order of every list is the same.
- A configured git or npm package that fails to install is now listed under `[Extension issues]` with the end of the command's output (`failed to install (<command> failed with code N: ...). Run "pig remove <source>" to remove it from settings.json.`), at startup and on `/reload`, as Pi lists it. The two startup lines `[pig] Reinstalled missing packages: ...` and `[pig] Could not install: ... (run pig update when online)` are gone: Pi prints neither, and the second one carried no error text.
- A start with a Node extension waits less before the extension's first handler runs. The host built the model catalog it hands the extension (about 2,500 models, 1.45 MB) on one processor; it now converts the models on up to eight processors, never more than the machine runs at once, and joins them in the catalog's own order, so the frame the extension receives is the same sequence of bytes as before. Measured with 30 warm starts of pig with a Node extension in json mode, on a loaded 192-processor host with the client held to four processors: the first reply began after 317 ms (median), now 275 ms; Pi with the same extension began after 336 ms. On a machine with one free processor the start takes as long as before. Extensions in Go, Python, Rust and Lisp, which ask the host for the catalog when they read it, are not affected.
- A tool's start and end are drawn through the frame throttle. Pi requests a frame at `tool_execution_start` and `tool_execution_end` (`interactive-mode.ts`, `this.ui.requestRender()`), which draws at most one frame every 16 ms; PiG drew a frame at once at both events, two frames 0.1 to 0.3 ms apart for every tool call, eleven frames for a prompt that reads four files where Pi-Bolt 1.2.1 draws four. The card's renderers still run at the event, as Pi's `updateDisplay` does, so a shell card's elapsed time starts where it did. On the fake-model benchmark an interactive session of five prompts runs 3.4 % fewer user instructions (two rounds of five sessions, both rounds).
- A typed key is matched against the keybindings without copying each action's keys. Every typed character is compared with every app action; the comparison copied the action's key list each time. The keys of one keybinding table are now kept and read. On the fake-model benchmark an interactive session of five prompts runs 1.4 % fewer user instructions.
- The start's heap return (D172) waits until the session has been idle for 500 ms. PiG returned the heap its start left free to the operating system right after the first frame, with one forced collection; a session that is prompted at once paid for that collection and then took the returned pages back for its first run. The return now waits like the idle collection after a run, and a run that starts first leaves it to that collection. A session left alone after its start returns the same memory half a second later. On the fake-model benchmark a session of one prompt runs 12.4 % fewer user instructions; a session of five prompts 0.4 % fewer.
- A spinner that animates while nothing else is drawn (the model has not answered yet, a tool is running) steps on time again, every 80 ms as in Pi. The wait of up to 40 ms that lets a streaming reply carry the spinner steps in its own frames (D619) now applies only while frames are being drawn; before, it also delayed every step of an idle spinner, and the longest time without output while waiting for a reply was a step and the wait instead of one step.
- Streaming frames are drawn on time. While a reply or a tool call streams in, PiG draws its frames 15 to 16 ms apart, as Pi does (Node cuts a timer delay to whole milliseconds), and on Linux it keeps the deadline of the next frame on a kernel timer, because the Go runtime timer fired up to a millisecond late there. The median time between frames falls from 16.7 ms to 15.6 ms, and the same stream is drawn in 5 to 7 % more frames.
- A chat-completions request is converted without copying its texts or the conversation. A replayed assistant message of one text block is sent as that block's string instead of a copy built for each request, and the messages that lead the request (the system prompt, the first system message's tools) are written into room the conversion leaves instead of every converted message being copied behind them. The request body is the same bytes. On the fake-model benchmark this commit, the next two (session details, hook messages) and nothing else lowered CPU per prompt by 4.0 % in a 20-prompt and a 40-prompt interactive session and user instructions by 4.3 % and 6.9 % (paired runs against the base, 7 and 4 pairs, measured on a build of the three changes together).
- Go hooks of the agent loop receive the run's own messages instead of a copy of the whole history made for every call. `PrepareRequest`, `FinishTurn`, `PrepareNextTurn`, and the before and after hooks of a tool call that runs alone or in a sequential batch get the run's array cut at its length: a hook that replaces a message in place now changes the request that follows and the rest of the run, as writing to `context.messages` does in Pi (with the copy that write was lost); a hook that appends still does not reach the run. The hooks of two or more tool calls executed in parallel can run at the same time, so each of those calls gets its own copy of the messages (before, the calls of one batch shared one copy): what such a hook writes stays its own. pig's own session hooks do not read these messages and extensions receive serialized copies, so nothing changes for the CLI or for extension SDKs.
- The before hooks of the tool calls of one assistant message that run in parallel receive the run's own messages (cut at their length), as Pi hands them `currentContext`: a hook that replaces a message in place now changes what the next call's before hook reads and the request that follows, as in Pi, where these hooks already run one after another. The tools and the after hooks of two or more parallel calls still receive a copy of the messages each, made once the before hooks have run, because Go runs them at the same time; what they write stays their own. pig's own session hooks do not read these messages and extensions receive serialized copies, so nothing changes for the CLI or for extension SDKs.
- A session without a file (`--no-session`, an in-memory session) no longer encodes a built-in tool's result details only to learn that they can be encoded. For the details of `read`, `bash`, `grep`, `find` and `ls` that is decided from their type, once; details of any other type are encoded as before. What the session holds is unchanged, and a session with a file writes the same lines. In the 40-prompt benchmark session this was 43 KB allocated per file read.
- A tool that produces the same large text again returns the string the conversation already holds. `read`, `grep`, `find`, `ls` and `bash` share an output of 4 KiB or more with an equal output produced earlier in the process (a file read again, a search or a listing repeated), so the conversation keeps that text once however often it was produced; tool results, request bodies and session entries are the same bytes. On the fake-model benchmark, where each prompt reads the same four files, the process's own memory after 40 prompts fell from 35.8 MB to 23.4 MB (33.5 % less, 7 of 7 paired runs against the base) and after 20 prompts from 24.9 MB to 20.1 MB (18.1 % less, 8 of 8); CPU per prompt stayed inside the noise (1.1 % more, 5 of 7 and 4 of 8 pairs) and user instructions rose by 5.0 % and 1.4 % because the smaller heap is collected more often. A session whose reads are all different gains nothing: there the process still holds each large text and its encoding (51 MB after 40 prompts of 160 different reads, the same as Pi-Bolt 1.2.1).
- RPC mode: the answer to a prompt that arrives while another prompt is still being admitted, for example two `prompt` commands written to standard input in one chunk, is now recorded as divergence D629 and described at the `prompt` command in the RPC command reference. PiG's behaviour is unchanged: it rejects the second prompt with `Agent is already processing. Specify streamingBehavior ('steer' or 'followUp') to queue the message.`. Pi 1.5.2 answers it `started`, never runs it, reports no error and emits an extra `agent_settled`; a test now runs the pinned Pi on the same input and fails when Pi's side changes.
- RPC mode holds its input from the start of a reload to the response of the command that awaited it, also while a reloaded extension's factory awaits a timer or I/O (D630). Pi reads stdin inside such a load: a prompt written then runs on the extension the reload has already invalidated and fails with the stale-context error, and the end of stdin exits without the response of the reloading command. In PiG the prompt runs on the reloaded extension after the reload, and the end of stdin is read after it.
- A reload ends a TypeScript extension whose handler holds its thread for more than 5 s across the reload, and loads it again in a new process. The command in flight on it is answered with an error that says the extension did not acknowledge a reload, and the reload says so in one line, `extension "<name>" did not acknowledge the reload within 5s and was restarted`: under Extension issues in the interactive `/reload` status, and on stderr in print, JSON and RPC mode. Pi has no such state, because its extensions run on the thread that runs the reload. This is the one case in which the host ends a running handler (D19; the exception to D56).
- The extensions guide has the section "Own compaction and continue after an overflow": an extension that writes its own summaries continues a turn after a provider overflow with the result of its `turn_end` and `agent_before_settle` handlers (`entries`, `continue`) or with a `session_before_compact` result, without a second user message and without the failed attempt, as in Pi. Nine cases compare PiG with the pinned Pi package (`TestExtensionOwnedCompactionContinuesAfterOverflow`, parity scenario `session/38-overflow-owner-boundaries`), and one conformance row covers the null and omitted draft members in the Go, Node, Python, Rust and Lisp SDKs, isolated, packed and fused. The context's doc comment in each SDK points to the handler result.
- Rust: `Provider` has the new public field `refresh_models_auth: Option<String>`, so a `Provider { .. }` struct literal must set it (`None` keeps Pi's default, `"credential"`). `Provider` has no `Default` (its `get_models`, `stream` and `stream_simple` have no meaningful default), so an extension that wants to avoid listing every optional field builds the value with `create_provider`, which sets it to `None`. <!-- feat: sdknative -->
- Go: `coding/extension.ProviderOAuth.ModifyModels` and `ExtensionOAuthConfig.ModifyModels` now return `([]Model, error)` so a failing hook is the model listing's error, as the exception of Pi's synchronous hook is. Rust: `OAuthProvider` has the new public fields `modify_models` and `uses_callback_server`; build one with `OAuthProvider::new(name, login)` and set the optional capabilities, since a struct literal without the new fields no longer compiles. <!-- feat: sdkprovidergaps -->
- The Go, Rust, Python and Lisp extension SDKs now answer the active model object (`ctx.GetModelInfo()`, `get_model_info`, `ctx-get-model-info`: name, context window, limits and prices) and the session id (`GetSessionID`, `session_manager.get_session_id`, `session-get-session-id`) from the host's state snapshot, as the Node runtime always did, instead of asking the host on every read. A read cost 57 µs through the host and costs 75 ns now, and an extension that reads the model twice per LLM call and the session id per prompt sends no host calls for them. The value is as fresh as the Node runtime's: the host pushes the snapshot before every dispatch, after `setModel`, and when the model or the session changes. A replacement session's context still asks the host. `getContextUsage` stays a host call, because Pi computes it live from the branch and a pushed copy goes stale after `waitForIdle`, `compact` and `navigateTree` and for a reader between requests.
- The Go, Rust, Python and Lisp extension SDKs also answer the session name and the session file (`GetSessionName`, `GetSessionFile`, the session manager's `getSessionName` and `getSessionFile`) from the host's state snapshot instead of a host call per read. A snapshot's session replaces both, so a replaced in-memory session clears the file the previous one had. The leaf id stays a host call, because it moves with every committed entry, which no state push announces.
- The root module zip that `go install github.com/MichaelKinsy/PiG/cmd/pig@<version>` downloads is about 460 KB smaller: it no longer holds the superseded SDK bundle copies `extensions/sdk-lisp/sdk.tgz` and the `.gz` twin directories of `extensions/sdk-py` and `extensions/sdk-rs` (463 KB), which the single `sdk.zst` frame replaced and no bundle reads. No SDK, bundle, staged copy or binary changes.
- A TypeScript extension project that imports `@michaelkinsy/pig-extension-types` type-checks `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent`, `pi-ai`, `pi-tui` and `pi-agent-core` against the Pi build PiG is pinned to, not against the installed release. The package ships `pi-pin.d.ts`, the pinned build's declarations as ambient modules, which `index.d.ts` references; it needs no `tsconfig` entry and works with `moduleResolution` `Node16` and `Bundler`. While the pin equals the published release the declarations are the release's. Once the pin is past it, the header of `pi-pin.d.ts` lists the exported declarations PiG has and that release lacks, and `make test-sdk-ts` prints them; the test that failed on such a difference now requires the bundle to equal the pinned build.
- `@michaelkinsy/pig-extension-types` declares the packages its declarations import as peer dependencies, at the versions the pinned Pi packages declare: `@anthropic-ai/sdk`, `@earendil-works/pi-codemode`, `@earendil-works/pi-mcp`, `@earendil-works/pi-schema`, `@earendil-works/pi-telemetry`, `@google/genai`, `marked`, `openai` and `typebox`. npm 7 and later and pnpm install them with the package. They are packages Pi's own install already brings, at the same versions while the pin equals the release, so the install adds nothing. `make vendor-sdk-ts-pin-declarations`, a step of `make pin-bump`, writes the bundle and the peer list.
- The Python, Rust and Lisp SDK tui helpers slice a line like Pi: an APC sequence before the slice (a cursor marker) is not carried into it. All four SDKs detect Alacritty by `TERM=alacritty` or `ALACRITTY_WINDOW_ID` as Pi does, and their Pi vectors are regenerated at the pin.
- An extension that clears a label with an empty string (`setLabel(id, "")`) now writes a label entry with `"label":""`, as Pi does. PiG wrote the entry without a `label` member. The label is cleared in both; a tool that reads session files now sees the empty string.
- Extension `setModel` takes a model object in every SDK, as Pi's `pi.setModel(model)` does. The session uses the object the extension passes, with the members it left on it (context window, input limits, base URL, API, compat, headers) and the credentials of its provider. PiG used to look the model up in its registry by provider and id and drop everything else. A registry model that an extension edits (Pi issue 9631: a `before_agent_start` handler that sets input limits) and a model built by hand for a provider PiG knows now work as under Pi. The session file still records the provider and the id only. Go: `Context.SetModel` takes the object (`map[string]any`) and the new `Context.SetModelNamed` takes the `provider/id` string. Python `set_model`, Rust `set_model` and Lisp `ctx-set-model` take the object or the string, and the string answers what it answered before.
- A model object an extension set stays the session's model until the registry's entry for its provider and id changes (the provider is registered again, `models.json` changes, a catalog refresh brings a new record). Then the session takes the registry's model.
- The `pig` binary is about 1.3 MB smaller: string ordering (`a.localeCompare(b)` parity: model lists, the `ls` tool, package and server lists) uses a fork of the root-locale collation of `golang.org/x/text` with only the tables the root locale reads, not the tables of every locale. The order of every string is the same: the fork is tested against x/text for every code point and for random strings. On the `ls` benchmark with 10,000 names, a sort takes 16.3 ms and allocates 2.60 MB, where it took 17.8 ms and 5.52 MB.
- The `pig` binary is about 3.5 MB smaller: the word-segmentation dictionaries (Chinese, Japanese, Thai, Lao, Khmer and Burmese) are 2.78 MB where they were 6.32 MB. They are stored as shared-prefix tries that are read in place, so nothing is decompressed, allocated or kept in memory. Word movement and deletion in the editor, double-click word selection and tool search segment text about three times faster than before (a Japanese line in 31 µs instead of 91 µs), the first Chinese or Japanese lookup in a process takes about 0.1 ms instead of 0.23 ms, a process holds less file-backed memory after its first segmentation, and the segmentation is unchanged.
- The `pig` binary is about 1.4 MB smaller (1.5 MB on Linux amd64 and Windows): `pig extension upgrade`, the startup offer for an extension written for an older SDK and `extensionsAutoUpgrade` no longer carry Go's type checker. They build `extensions/sdk/upgrade/driver` from the staged SDK with the Go toolchain that builds the extension, and run it. The plan, the report and the error text stay the same. The first analysis after a Go or SDK update compiles that program (a few seconds on an empty Go build cache); each later analysis takes about 0.1 s longer than before.
- `Value.Check` and `Value.Errors` do less work: `minLength` and `maxLength` of an ASCII text no longer convert the text, `uniqueItems` on strings and objects allocates up to 90% less and takes about half the time, and `Errors` builds its messages only for the checks that fail.
- The `pig` binary is about 0.42 to 0.60 MB smaller (linux_amd64 0.60 MB): sorts of short lists and of lists that no timed path sorts at length use one shared sort routine instead of one copy of the sort per element type. Sorts of long lists on timed paths (session load, the model picker, file suggestions) keep the standard library's code, so no sort on a timed path takes longer. The sorted order is the same.
- The `pig` binary is about 500 KB smaller: the host checks `Value.Check` and `Value.Errors` with one walker, as TypeBox does, and no longer links a generic JSON Schema validator.
- The release binary is 49,926 B smaller: the full highlight.js grammar snapshot is stored as one zstd frame (208,419 B) instead of a gzip stream (258,345 B) and decodes to the same text. The first highlight of a language outside the eager set is faster (15.0 ms instead of 20.4 ms).
- The `pig` binary and an embedder's program are about 16 KB smaller: the Go SDK's lookup of the member order of a decoded JSON object sorts its entries with one small routine instead of a copy of the standard library's sort compiled for that entry type. The order of the entries, and so every answer the lookup gives, is the same.
- The release binary is 544,768 B smaller: the embedded Node runtime (4,740,074 B) is stored as zstd frames written by the same pinned zstd command at its highest level that writes every other embedded frame, 4,195,160 B, and unpacks to the same files. The first start of a Node extension in a fresh cache takes the same time as before (268.6 ms against 276.0 ms median over ten paired runs of a cold start, ready included), with the same memory.
- The `pig` binary is 344,064 bytes smaller (64,368,903 to 64,024,839 stripped on linux/amd64). Each embedded SDK (Go, Python, Rust and Lisp) is one solid zstd frame of its files instead of a gzip per file (the Lisp SDK, a gzip tar): the Go SDK is 427,851 bytes (was 547,801), Python 244,679 (297,245), Rust 381,912 (470,923) and Lisp 230,586 (260,343). Staging decodes the frame once and writes every file from that buffer: staging the Go SDK allocates 2.6 MB in about 12 ms where it allocated 13.0 MB in about 35 ms, and staging the four SDKs together grows the process by 6.3 MB of resident memory at most instead of 7.9 MB. The staged files are the same bytes as before.
- A start whose staged SDKs are current no longer hashes the embedded SDKs: the staging hash of each SDK is generated with it, so the check reads one marker per language and decodes nothing (a warm `EnsureSynced` took 1.6 to 2.4 ms and 1,950 allocations, and takes 0.13 ms and 69). The Go, Python and Rust staged directories get new names once (`sdk-<hash>`, `sdk-py-<hash>`, `sdk-rs-<hash>`), because their hash now covers the files' text, as the Lisp hash already did; the first start after the upgrade stages them again, and extension builds whose SDK files did not change stay reachable.
- The Go SDK module `extensions/sdk` is unchanged: its `Source` and `BundledFiles()` are what the published module has. The root module packs the module's sources itself, in `internal/gosdkbundle`, which `automation/gen/packsdk` generates from `extensions/sdk` (a zstd frame, `sdk.zst`, with the file list and the staging hash); the Python, Rust and Lisp SDK packages hold the same kind of frame. In those three packages `Source` holds the one file `sdk.zst`, `BundledFiles()` names the staged files themselves, and the new `StagedHash()` returns the hash the staged directory is marked with. None of them decodes the frame: `coding/extension/pigsdk` does. `make sdk-bundles` regenerates every frame and list.
- The embedded `CHANGELOG.md` is stored as a zstd frame (318 KB, 38 KB smaller than the gzip it replaces). The startup What's New check and `/changelog` decode it in about 2.8 ms instead of 9.7 ms and allocate 1.2 MB instead of 3.3 MB.
- The root module zip that `go install github.com/MichaelKinsy/PiG/cmd/pig@version` downloads is 52 MB smaller, 129.5 MB instead of 181.9 MB uncompressed. The committed Node runtime source tree, the documentation tree, and test and tooling data that no build reads now sit in data-only nested modules: they stay in the repository and are read by path in a checkout, but the module zip omits them. The `pig` binary is unchanged (the same SHA-256), and `make module-size` now holds the zip to a 133 MB budget.
- The `pig` binary is about 430 KB smaller (Linux amd64): the 52 pages of the agent docs bundle are embedded as one compressed block instead of 610 KB of plain text. A start no longer hashes the pages to name the bundle directory (the names and the digest are generated with the block), which saves about 1.5 ms of CPU and 39 KB of allocations; `pig docs sync` and the first start of a build decode the block once (about 1.6 ms) and keep nothing of it. The docs bundle on disk is unchanged.
- Startup reaches the first interactive frame about 1.2 ms sooner (22.1 ms to 20.9 ms median on a loaded 2-socket Xeon host pinned to one core, n=150 interleaved) with the same screen: the text-width tables filled a 128 KB cache of the Basic Multilingual Plane for the TUI and a second one for the extension SDK before the program started, and now fill a 256-code-point block when the first width lookup lands in it, so a first frame builds a few blocks and a process that never measures a string builds none. Width and wrapping benchmarks are unchanged within noise.
- The extension host's state push worker ends when it has nothing to push instead of staying parked, so a session with a view client attached and no mount holds no goroutine for it.
- The main screen's per-line reset costs less: a line is checked for images and cursor markers in one pass and the marker strip no longer adds a scan or an allocation, so a styled row and a row with a stray marker are each one allocation and faster than before the cursor-marker strip, with the same output.
- Tooling: a failed `make interface-gaps` over a mirror that is not the pinned build now says so and names `make upstream-mirror`. Before, a `.upstream/current` left at another Pi commit (as a `make test-carried-oracles` run left it at the time) made the check read that Pi and report its reopened rows as seven gaps of the tree.
- durable: the Cloudflare host (`durable/core/host/cf`), `durable/interop` and the Kubernetes benchmark image's pi-durable project install Pi's durable and chord packages (`pi-durable`, `chord`, `pi-ai`, `pi-codemode`, `pi-schema`, `pi-telemetry`) from `third_party/pi-packs`, the `npm pack` outputs of the pinned Pi source build, through `file:` dependencies whose locks carry each pack's sha512; before, their `package.json` named the npm 1.5.2 release, which lacks suspendable work and chord events, and only the tests swapped the pinned build in. `make pin-bump` regenerates the packs (`make vendor-pi-packs`), and `make pin-check` fails when a pack differs from its manifest, a lock resolves a Pi package from the registry, or a `package.json` names a Pi package by version. `make link-durable-host` and the frozen durable closures are gone.
- sdk-ts: `make test-sdk-ts` fails, naming each declaration, when the exported declarations of the pinned Pi source build differ from the published release the peer dependency names (`extensions/sdk-ts/testdata`, a checksum-verified snapshot; `make vendor-sdk-ts-declarations` writes it).
- `pig --version` and `pig -v` now print Pi's own version, the package version of the pinned Pi build, exactly as `pi --version` does, so a launcher that checks Pi's version (T3 Code's Pi provider rejected the composite version) accepts PiG. PiG's release is in `pig version`, which prints the PiG release and the Pi version in separate fields; the help and diagnostics banner and the interactive startup line still show `<PiG release>+<Pi release>`. Self-update, the installer and the release scripts read the release from `pig version`.
- A `/reload`, and `ctx.reload()` in every mode, now ends the view mounts (`ctx.ui.mountView` and its forms in the other SDKs) of the extensions it reloads: every attached view client, the terminal included, is sent each such mount once more in state `broken` with reason `owner_gone`, and the reloaded extension mounts its keys again under a new epoch. Before, the mount of the instance before the reload stayed live and drawn, and the reloaded extension's mount of the same key failed with `invalid` ("already mounted"). An extension that mounts when it starts or when a client arrives needs no change; one that took its old mount over through `viewState(key)` now finds it `broken` and mounts again. An intent raised on the ended mount is refused. A client of the view endpoint keeps its connection and its attachment across the reload, as before.
- An image in a mounted view counts against a client's snapshot size and no longer against its text limit. Before, every client that takes 65,536 bytes of text refused an image of more than 49,152 bytes. The terminal takes an image of about 195,000 bytes; the web client's snapshot limit is 1,048,576 bytes.
- A view that asks for the keyboard gets it only from an empty editor. While you are typing, the view is shown and the focus stays in the editor; the extension is told why.
- Two panels that an extension mounts are no longer drawn one under the other in the terminal: they are tabs. One panel without a title is drawn as before.
- An intent handler may redraw its own mount before it answers (D614). An update the answering handler makes to the mount its intent came from belongs to the answer: the intent settles `done` instead of `stale`, and RPC mode writes the `ui_view` event of that update before the reply to `ui_view_intent`. A change by another hand while the handler answers still settles the intent `stale`. No SDK call and no carrier message changed.
- `uiview.Registry.OnAbilities` registers any number of functions, in registration order, and returns the function that removes its argument; it replaced the function registered before.
- The demo extension of `examples/ui-view-web` redraws inside the answer; it no longer defers the update with a timer.
- A reload, a second session, `/resume` and `/fork` no longer read the Go SDK's files again to find the built cell of an extension. A process reads and hashes the SDK that this pig staged under `<config root>/state/pigsdk` once (212 files, 2.1 MB for an installed pig) and keeps the hash with each file's size and modification time; a later load walks the directory and checks those, reads no file, and looks for the cell under the kept hash. On the repository's larger SDK tree (424 files) a lookup takes 2.2 ms instead of 11 ms and 0 file reads instead of 424. A file that changed size or modification time, or was added, removed or renamed, makes the hash be computed again from the files, so an edited SDK still selects another cell and rebuilds it. The SDK of a source checkout (`extensions/sdk` found from the working directory, `PIG_SDK_GO_ROOT`) is still hashed by content on every load. A one-shot `pig -p` gains nothing, since its single load reads the SDK once. One edit is not seen: one that keeps both the size and the modification time of a file already older than two seconds (a tool that restores times); pig's own staging, the only writer of the staged SDK, replaces the directory with newly dated files. A build never uses the kept hash: it hashes the tree under its build lock, and again when the compiler returns.
- The reference web client of plugin views (`examples/ui-view-web`) draws what a view says about layout and colour: `gap`, `align` and each child's `stack` entry of an `hstack` or `vstack` (so cells with `basis: 0, grow: 1` are columns of one width), the padding of `box`, `text` and `truncated-text`, `bg` and `color` theme tokens, and the view's `theme` overrides. A cell is `1ch` wide and one line high. Markdown nodes are drawn as markdown; their text is never parsed as HTML and only `http`, `https` and `mailto` links are followed.
- The reference web client shows panel mounts beside the chat, side by side or as tabs. A panel behind another is still updated; which panel is shown is the user's choice.
- `make ci-chord-web` also runs the page tests of `examples/ui-view-web` in Chromium; a missing browser or Node fails them there.
- The reference web client of plugin views (`examples/ui-view-web`) draws a view as controls instead of text. A node is the control its kind and the role and states of its `a11y` record make it: a `mouse-region` is a button, or a native checkbox, switch or radio with its checked state; a `text` with the role `heading` is a heading; a `select-list` is a listbox of rows, or a row of tabs; a `lines` node with `progress` is a progress bar and with `list` a list in columns; a `grid` is a grid; a `loader` is a status with a spinner; a mount of the `dialog` slot is a modal dialog. An intent of the mount is a button that reads the intent's verb in words. The page sends the same `ui_view_intent` commands for a click or a key as before; a golden file of them is compared in the tests.
- The reference web client draws a mount's `drawing`: it states both profiles (4096 shapes, 1048576 pixels) and `snapshotBytes` 4194304, draws a scene as one SVG element with every shape kind and theme-token colours, and makes each region a focusable element that raises its intent for a click, a key, a press, a release and a drag. A shape with a `key` keeps its element across updates, so a scene that is sent again moves in place. Before, a mount with a drawing reached the page as its fallback.
- The reference web client labels a mount with its `title`, fires key bindings while the focus is inside the mount and shows the named ones as buttons with their key, moves the focus for `request: update`, and takes no focus from a text field that holds text: it reports `unfocused` instead, and a dialog then opens without being modal until the user enters it. It states the claim `input.bindings = [key]` and the node kinds `loader` and `grid`.
- The reference web client updates in place: every element whose node is still in the view is kept, so a state changes by its transition and the focus, the selection and typed text stay.
- The reference web client's look is a default stylesheet of custom properties (`--view-*`: type scale, spacing, radii, colours for light and dark, motion that stops under `prefers-reduced-motion`), which a `--theme` directory overrides. A cell of a view is 8 by 16 px (`--view-col`, `--view-row`), no longer `1ch` by one line. While the chat holds no line the panels and the prompt are one centred column, and with `--connect` the panels take the page. The line of the carrier's numbers under the prompt is shown only when the address has `?debug`.
- `docs/ui-view-carrier.md` proposes how a client fills the argument of a gesture on a drawing's region: `x`, `y`, `dx`, `dy`, `gesture` and `region`, each only when the intent's declared shape names it.
- The reference web client draws a mount's `title` as the heading of its card; a mount without one keeps the small caption `<plugin> / <key>`. The page under a modal dialog is dimmed by the new token `--view-backdrop` (black at 20 % in the light scheme, 30 % in the dark one), a loader stands 8 px under the node before it, and under a panel taller than the window the prompt stays in sight at the window's lower edge.
- The reference web client says less when a mount ends: nothing for a mount its extension finished or removed, and for a mount that broke one line by its title (`<title> closed: its extension stopped.`) that goes when the same key is mounted again, as after `/reload`. Before, it wrote `<plugin>/<key> <state> (<reason>)` for every end and kept the line; that form is now written only with `?debug`. A dialog stands on the new token `--view-surface-raised`, a step above a card in the dark scheme.

### Deprecated

- Go: the `SessionID`, `SessionFile`, `Model`, `ThinkingLevel`, `ActiveTools` and `SystemPrompt` fields of `*sdk.AgentSession` still hold what the session had when `ctx.CreateAgentSession` returned, but they are deprecated. Use the methods that read the session's current value: `CurrentSessionID()`, `CurrentSessionFile()`, `CurrentModel()`, `CurrentThinkingLevel()`, `GetActiveToolNames()` and `CurrentSystemPrompt()`, each returning `(value, error)`. The live reads cannot reuse the field names, because a Go field and method cannot share a name, so `SessionID()`, `Model()` and the others do not exist on `*sdk.AgentSession`.
- Lisp: `agent-session-session-id`, `-session-file`, `-model`, `-thinking-level`, `-active-tools` and `-system-prompt` still return what the session held when `ctx-create-agent-session` returned, but they are deprecated. Use `agent-session-current-session-id`, `-current-session-file`, `-current-model`, `-current-thinking-level`, `agent-session-get-active-tool-names` and `agent-session-current-system-prompt`, which ask the host for the current value. The live reads cannot reuse the old names, because a Lisp function has one definition per symbol, so `agent-session-session-id` and the others keep returning the creation snapshot.
- Python: the `session_id`, `session_file`, `model`, `thinking_level`, `active_tools` and `system_prompt` attributes of an `AgentSession` still hold what the session had when it was created, but reading them raises a `DeprecationWarning` (silent by default outside `__main__`; under `-W error` or a `filterwarnings = error` pytest setup the read raises, and so do `hasattr(session, "model")`, `getattr` and `inspect.getmembers(session)` on those names; assignment never warns, and the values are no longer listed by `vars(session)`). Use the properties that read the current value from the host: `current_session_id`, `current_session_file`, `current_model`, `current_thinking_level`, `get_active_tool_names()` and `current_system_prompt`.
- Rust: the `session_id`, `session_file`, `model`, `thinking_level`, `active_tools` and `system_prompt` fields of `AgentSession` still hold what the session had when it was created, but are marked `#[deprecated]`. Use the methods that read the current value, returning `io::Result` (named `current_*`, not `session_id()` and the like, to match the Go, Python and Lisp names): `current_session_id()`, `current_session_file()`, `current_model()`, `current_thinking_level()`, `get_active_tool_names()` and `current_system_prompt()`.

### Removed

- The Go package `chord/host` (Chord v1: `CreateHost`, `Cell`, `Derived`, the v1 contracts, links, host manager and Node facet loader) is gone, as Pi removed Chord v1 when Chord v2 became its root export. Use `chord/next/{contracts,data,state,registries,link,host,store}` and `chord/nextnode`. The root package `chord` no longer has replicated state (`NewReplicatedState`, `AttachReplicatedStateSource`, `ReplicatedState` and its delivery types); it keeps `AggregateError`, `SetUncaughtErrorReporter`, strict JSON and watches.
- The retired `deepseek-v3.2` and `deepseek-v4-flash` from the Qwen Token Plan Team providers; use `deepseek-v4-flash-0731` or `deepseek-v4.1-flash`. <!-- fix: 1397070024 -->
- `coding.ResolveModelScope` from the Go SDK, which printed the scope warnings to stderr itself. Use `coding.ResolveModelScopeWithDiagnostics` and report its `Diagnostics`.
- `PIG_VERSION_FORMAT` is gone: `pig --version` always prints Pi's version, so the opt-in has nothing left to switch.

### Fixed

- Aborting a compaction or a session-tree move while extensions were handling `session_before_compact` or `session_before_tree` no longer drops the handler's reply and keeps every later extension from hearing about it. As in Pi, each handler now receives the event in order, `event.signal` aborts for the one that is running, and a handler dispatched after the abort starts with the signal already aborted. A `{ cancel: true }`, summary, instructions or label returned after a tree move was aborted is honoured. <!-- fix: 05b3416ad99, 6b778e70d74 -->
- A `session_tree` handler is no longer cancelled, and later extensions no longer miss the event, when the context of the tree navigation ended while it ran. As in Pi, the event reaches every extension after the leaf moved. <!-- fix: 41063244c43, c3342406bf2 -->
- Aborting a compaction or a branch summary while an extension's `session_before_compact` or `session_before_tree` handler awaits a host call, such as a dialog, a notification or a session read, no longer fails that call in the Go, Node, Python, Rust and Lisp extension SDKs. The abort aborts the handler's `event.signal` and nothing else, as in Pi: the pending call and later calls return their results, and the handler's reply is kept. <!-- fix: 9a9b153d6bf, 4139cda4739 -->
- A tool call whose run had already aborted when it reached an extension, a direct call of the tool or an abort that landed after the agent's gate, failed with `context canceled` without the extension ever seeing it. It now reaches the tool with its signal already aborted, as it does in Pi, so a tool that checks `signal.aborted` first (the subagent example returns its five aborted task results) answers for itself, in the Go, Node, Python, Rust and Lisp SDKs, isolated, packed and fused. The tool's host calls are answered, the 3 s grace period of an aborted call runs from the call's start, and a tool that does not settle still ends as `Operation aborted`; a connection that is closing or closed takes no call. A call whose frames cannot be queued within that period (the writer's queue stays full) ends as `Operation aborted`; a frame already queued waits for its write as every request does and ends with the connection's heartbeat failure when the peer stops reading. <!-- fix: a91bfc0eb4 --> <!-- cause: the host treated an ended context as a reason not to enter the tool, so the tool_call request failed with the context's error, where Pi runs tool.execute with an aborted signal and only the agent loop's own gates skip the call --> <!-- tests: TestSubagentExampleChildLifecycle, TestEndedToolCallReachesTheExtensionWithItsSignalAborted, TestEndedToolCallDoesNotLengthenShutdownOrReplacement, TestConformance_ToolCalledAbortedEntersWithItsSignalAborted -->
- An interactive turn stopped with Escape, a signal or an extension's `ctx.abort()` is saved with the text Pi saves: "Operation aborted", or "Aborted after N retry attempt(s)" when an automatic retry was running. The session file, an extension's `turn_end` and `agent_end` handlers and the next request carried the provider's text before; print, JSON and RPC modes keep the provider's text, as in Pi. <!-- fix: 6aa94467d3d -->
- An extension that calls `ctx.abort()` from an event handler in interactive mode no longer hangs the session: the call returns at once, the turn ends aborted and the next prompt runs, in the Node, Go, Python and Rust SDKs. Before, the turn never ended and no later prompt was answered; Escape and print, JSON and RPC modes were not affected. Messages queued while the turn ran go back to the editor instead of running after the abort, as in Pi. Affects 0.2.0 through 0.7.0. <!-- fix: df5e3e87ffc, a079f7223f5 -->
- A command's reply is no longer held back by calls or dialogs an extension handler starts after it began to wait (`Conn.readLoop` seals `ackHold` on a non-`host_call` `blocked` report and records `ackCounted` on `Envelope` so only calls read before the report hold or release the acknowledgment). <!-- fix: ff7b27274e, 6c102b39a7 --> <!-- cause: ackHold counted host calls and blocked:host_call announcements by when Conn.readLoop read them rather than whether the handler sent them before its blocked report, so a post-report call or announcement read before stateCh was drained raised unapplied or announced and falsely held the acknowledgment -->
- Starting PiG with an agent directory that cannot be made (a regular file where a parent directory should be, a parent that cannot be written, a read-only file system) now ends where Pi ends: with the session directory of a new session, the error is Node's own `ENOTDIR: not a directory, mkdir '<agent>/sessions/--<cwd>--'` (with `--no-session` Pi's project trust store reports it for the agent directory), and a program that gives `CreateAgentSession` its own session manager is no longer refused with `open auth storage at <path>`: the credential store opens, and the first credential or settings write reports the mkdir error, as Pi's does. PiG stopped at the credential store with its own text, read a settings file behind an unmakeable directory as a load error where Pi reads none, wrapped the session directory's error in `sessionmanager: mkdir` and tried to make a session directory that exists as a file. Since PiG 0.2.0 for the credential store (v0.7.0 is the last release). <!-- tests: ai/auth_unmakeable_directory_upstream_test.go::TestNewAuthStorageOpensWhereTheDirectoryCannotBeMadeAndTheFirstWriteReports, coding/sdk_unmakeable_agent_dir_test.go::TestCreateAgentSessionRejectsWithNodesMkdirErrorForTheDefaultSessionDirectory, coding/cli/unmakeable_agent_dir_modes_test.go::TestStartupMakesTheDirectoryOfANewSessionBeforeAnythingElse, coding/cli/unmakeable_agent_dir_modes_test.go::TestPrintAndRPCModeEndWithNodesMkdirErrorWhereTheAgentDirectoryCannotBeMade, internal/codingagent/settings_unmakeable_directory_oracle_test.go::TestSettingsOfAnAgentDirectoryThatCannotBeMadeRecordNoLoadErrorAndTheFirstWriteReportsMkdir --> <!-- fix: a984cccf08 -->
- ai: an images API provider now refuses a model of another api with `Mismatched api: <model api> expected <api>` before it runs, as Pi's images registry does; GitHub Copilot and OpenAI Codex logins report `Login cancelled` when the login is cancelled while a prompt or request is in flight, and GitHub Copilot login errors are no longer prefixed. <!-- fix: 274fef902d -->
- ai: `Models.GenerateImages` given a model of another api than its images provider's ends with the error `Mismatched api: <model api> expected <api>`, as Pi's `generateImages` returns the images registry's refusal as an error result; PiG 0.4.0 to 0.7.0 ran the provider with that model. <!-- fix: cb160949e7 -->
- Encoding every built-in model, as an extension host does when it attaches, no longer leaves 1.2 MB of per-model comparison encodings on the heap: a built-in model's baseline is kept as a 32-byte SHA-256 digest in a fixed array, so the heap retained after the encoding is 1.07 MB, not 2.27 MB, and the encoding allocates 0.2 MB less. Record lookups cost what they did (`ResolveCatalogRecord` 3.1 ns, a pass over all 1,629 rows 5.6 µs); hashing makes `CatalogModelJSON` over all models about 1 µs per model slower (12.7 ms against 11.0 ms, a pass over all 1,629 models). <!-- fix: a966fc9a7c -->
- `ctx.reload()` in print and RPC mode, and `Session.Reload` for SDK callers, now fail with `Wait for the current response to finish before reloading.` while a response is running, and with `Wait for compaction to finish before reloading.` during compaction or tree navigation, instead of shutting the extensions down under a running tool, which then failed with a stale-context error. A refused reload leaves the extensions and the running tool's context untouched, and the extension sees the error in every SDK. <!-- fix: 0f8bc0f0de -->
- `PI_STARTUP_BENCHMARK=1` disposes the session runtime after it stops interactive mode, so extensions receive `session_shutdown` and release their timers and sockets, as in Pi. <!-- fix: 26a08b0995 -->
- The default output limit leaves 15% of the estimated input unused (at least 4,096 tokens), and near a full window requests at most 32,768 output tokens, as in Pi, so OpenRouter's higher token count for the same input no longer makes it reject the request with a 400 that PiG then treated as a context overflow and compacted. <!-- fix: 60473d7e53 -->
- Requests to Claude Sonnet 5 no longer send `temperature`, as in Pi: the catalog marks the Sonnet 5 models on an Anthropic-messages provider as not supporting it. <!-- fix: 787c3547c4 -->
- `pig config` loads the remaps in `keybindings.json`, as `/settings` and the `--resume` picker already did. <!-- fix: 8934633d04 -->
- Ctrl+V pastes files, images and text on Windows and WSL as well as Alt+V (terminals that pass Ctrl+V to the program as a raw key did nothing before), as in Pi. <!-- fix: 8b792f9bd1 -->
- The OpenAI Responses API now gets the session-affinity header `session-id` instead of `session_id`, as in Pi, because nginx drops underscored headers by default and Envoy can reject them, which lost cache affinity behind such proxies. The Completions API still sends `session_id`. <!-- fix: bf094afb3e -->
- `pig mcp list` sends the token of the provider named by a server's `auth.provider` (Radius, for example), refreshed when expired, so a signed-in provider's server no longer shows as needing sign-in. The hint then reads `/login <provider> in pig`, `--json` carries `authProvider`, and `pig mcp login` and `pig mcp logout` point to `/login` and `/logout` instead of failing with "does not use OAuth". <!-- fix: c807fb7058 -->
- MCP servers that frame server-sent events with a lone CR (or a CRLF split across reads) now deliver their events, as in Pi; the call used to fail with "stream ended without a response". <!-- fix: ce7dae9221 -->
- An unreachable llama.cpp server now reports `Could not reach llama.cpp server at <url>: <cause>` (in `/login llama.cpp`, `/llama` and the model refresh) instead of `fetch failed`, as in Pi. <!-- fix: fa4a558a1b -->
- A call that fails before the provider has a response stream (an HTTP error answered by Gemini, Vertex or Mistral, or a payload hook that rejects the request on an OpenAI-style or Azure model) now reports `durationMs` from the start of the call, as Pi does. The failed message was timed from after the call: a program that reads the module's own stream (`ai.APIModuleStream`) saw no `durationMs` whenever a millisecond boundary fell inside the call, which every real network request crosses, and `0` otherwise, and a session saw a value measured by the stream that forwards it, not by the call. <!-- fix: a97881e371 -->
- `pig update --models` warns about a provider whose OAuth login can no longer be refreshed (`Warning: skipped model catalog for <provider>: ...`, with the `pig auth login <provider>` command to sign in again) and finishes successfully; it fails only for other refresh errors, and the failure lists only those. <!-- fix: 6f553cab69 -->
- Azure OpenAI models now keep OpenAI's long-context price tier, so requests above 272K input tokens are costed at Azure's long-context rates (Pi #11948). <!-- fix: 9624fc45422bb2d12b1be3f4ff1d8206e558d682 -->
- Anthropic and Bedrock no longer send `strict: "prefer"` tools strict again on every request after Claude rejected them for exceeding its strict tool limits, which cost a rejected request (400) per turn. Later requests with the same session id now send those tools non-strict right away, until `CleanupSessionResources(sessionID)` (Pi #11626). <!-- fix: 9624fc45422bb2d12b1be3f4ff1d8206e558d682 -->
- Fullscreen: copying a selection with OSC 52 (when no clipboard tool is set, as an extension screen does unless it supplies `copySelection`), entering and leaving the alternate screen, and switching the terminal's light/dark reports now wait for a frame that is being written instead of writing at the same time, so a copy or a switch no longer lands among the bytes of a frame. An extension screen's start and stop show and hide the cursor through the same path. <!-- fix: 84adf0cc98699c3b708e18bd2275f047eeb65622 --> <!-- cause: the alternate screen's own writes held its render lock but not the terminal writer's lock that frames and cursor writes take, because the writer lock was added for cursor and raw writes and these seven writes were not among the ones it was applied to -->
- Anthropic Messages request bodies now have the member order of the bodies Pi sends. PiG wrote four objects of the request body with their members in another order than Pi's `JSON.stringify` does; the content was the same. A text block carrying the conversation's cache breakpoint was `type, cache_control, text` (Pi: `type, text, cache_control`). An image source, in a user message or in a tool result, was `data, media_type, type` (Pi: `type, media_type, data`). The request's optional members were `system, tools, tool_choice, metadata, thinking, output_config, temperature` (Pi: `system, temperature, tools, thinking, output_config, metadata, tool_choice`). A tool choice object sent by an extension had its keys sorted, where Pi sends the extension's own order. This held for every provider that uses the Anthropic Messages API: Anthropic with an API key or OAuth, GitHub Copilot, OpenRouter, OpenCode, Vercel AI Gateway, MiniMax, Fireworks, Cloudflare AI Gateway and custom base URLs. Anthropic's prompt caching documentation says a cache hit needs an identical prompt prefix and names the key order of `tool_use` blocks as part of it; it does not say whether the member order of the objects fixed here is. <!-- fix: 69158e9e9e -->
- A server killed in the middle of importing or deleting the data of one address (an app built with the kit keeps the address's records in two SQLite stores, the plugins' and the server host's, where Pi has one) no longer leaves it partly imported or deleted: the import or delete writes a record of itself, with the address's old data, to `server/imports/` before its first commit and removes it after its second, and the next start undoes an interrupted import (the address is as it was) or completes an interrupted delete before serving anything, and reports it as an app error of kind `interrupted_data_change`. A record that cannot be used blocks only its own address and is reported. <!-- fix: 4477d23ffb0004c18b55739798666986adba74f8 --> <!-- cause: PiG split Pi's one server commit into two stores and kept an undo only for a failure the process survives, so a kill between the two commits left the address partly imported or deleted, and no test killed the process there -->
- A worker's or server's data archive is now one format, Pi's: PiG's export writes one `store.archive` (the plugins' records and the kit's tables together) and one `server.archive` (both hosts' records), and Pi imports it, where Pi refused the `kit.archive` and `kit-server.archive` entries PiG wrote before. PiG imports an archive of either of them by routing the kit's parts into its own store and each host's records to the host that serves them; the two former entries are no longer read. <!-- fix: 960bf047f986eb27911e2f472e86c41ed92c74c7 --> <!-- cause: PiG split Pi's one store into two and wrote the kit's half as entries of its own that Pi's import refuses, and no test ran an archive PiG made through Pi's own unpack -->
- Importing an archive that Pi made now keeps the file index: a worker's files of an archive Pi exported arrive with their versions, folders and summary, where only the file bytes came before and the Go `Files` facet listed nothing. `CopyFiles` writes its copy's index where the `Files` facet reads it. <!-- fix: e90cd5ff37f4478cc01cd64acc70ef8fb1c79838 --> <!-- cause: PiG keeps the kit's Files tables in a second store beside the plugins' but imported Pi's single store archive whole into the plugins' store, and no test ran an archive Pi itself made through the import -->
- A `tool_call` handler that assigns a new object to `event.input` now gives it to the next handlers of the call, as in Pi, in Node extensions and in the Go, Python and Lisp SDKs; before, the next handler read the original input (in Node, Go and Python from v0.5.0 to v0.7.0, and in Lisp in v0.7.0). The call itself still runs with the input it carried, as in Pi, so nothing a released extension could rely on is lost; a Rust handler keeps its own behaviour, which is unchanged in every released version: the Rust SDK holds the event as one value, so assigning the input and editing it in place are the same edit and the tool runs with what the handler left. <!-- fix: 85791f823c --> <!-- cause: the reply protocol had one member for the input, meant for in-place edits the tool must receive, so an assigned input had no way across the process boundary and was dropped as no edit -->
- `/llama`: a request to the llama.cpp server or to Hugging Face starts its own 15-second timeout only when its caller has no deadline or a later one. When the caller's deadline was due at the same instant, both timers ran and either could fire first, so a model registry refresh that did not answer could end as `Could not connect to the server.` where Pi shows `Model catalog refresh timed out.`; in Pi the caller's timer is created first and fires first. No user on Linux or macOS sees a change: their clocks advance between the start of the catalog sync and its request, so the request never had a timer of its own (measured on Linux: Pi's text in 450 of 450 real-time runs before the change). The other text was reachable only on a clock that does not advance between those two calls; no run was made on such a platform. <!-- fix: 3a220c1b33d525b035a6fd7a11f8fc8ab5443ae7 -->
- Resource reload: an override function (skills, prompt templates, themes, extensions, context files, system prompt) that calls the resource loader, and a project-trust callback or extension load that calls `ExtendResources` or `Close`, no longer block forever on the loader's operation lock; the call runs inside the reload in progress, as Pi's unlocked reload does. Reloads that overlap from outside still wait for each other (D632). <!-- fix: 68dfec5e1afa801b31ee0ad11a3304fc26800f22 -->
- Settings: a change whose save failed (for example while another process held the settings lock) is now saved by the next successful save of the same file, as Pi does; before, it stayed in effect until the restart and was then lost. <!-- fix: e5f76fefdec454b13f8bfc1a44c72e4a1e166c3d -->
- Settings: an extension settings storage whose lock callback changes a setting no longer blocks forever; the change is saved after the save in progress, as in Pi. <!-- fix: e5f76fefdec454b13f8bfc1a44c72e4a1e166c3d -->
- `pig --list-models` now checks credentials again before it prints, as Pi does. When `auth.json` cannot be read (for example it is not valid JSON) the run warns `Availability refresh: <error>`, reports the error and exits with status 1 instead of printing a table and exiting 0; a check that takes longer than 15 s ends the same way with a timeout error. <!-- fix: b91a45414fe5a88a545de56aca92416787e2e5ef -->
